config.title: Lippincott Pathology Block 1 QBank
config.subtitle: Cell injury, inflammation, repair/regeneration, immunopathology, developmental/genetic disease, skeletal muscle, and nervous system pathology (Rubin's Pathology Ch 1-4, 6, 27-28)

questions.stem: Bone marrow cells from an organ donor are cultured in vitro at 37°C in the presence of recombinant erythropoietin. A photomicrograph of a typical "burst-forming unit" is shown in the image. This colony, committed to the erythrocyte pathway of differentiation, represents an example of which of the following physiologic adaptations to transmembrane signaling?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin signaling drives proliferation of erythroid precursors, producing hyperplasia (an increase in cell number) as seen in burst-forming units. This is the same mechanism underlying the erythroid hyperplasia observed in people living at high altitude, where hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin release. Hypertrophy, by contrast, is an increase in cell size rather than number and does not apply to a proliferating colony of progenitor cells. Hyperplasia and hypertrophy often occur together in tissues capable of division but are mechanistically distinct.
keypoints: ⭐ Erythropoietin is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia
Burst-forming units (BFU-E) are early erythroid progenitors that give rise to colony-forming units (CFU-E)
Hyperplasia requires cells capable of mitotic division; permanent cells (e.g., neurons, cardiac myocytes) cannot undergo hyperplasia
questions.imageAlt: Photomicrograph of a burst-forming erythroid unit (BFU-E) colony
questions.imageCaption: Erythroid progenitor colony grown in vitro with erythropoietin

questions.stem: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents to the emergency room with 12 hours of severe abdominal pain. The pain radiates to the back and is associated with an urge to vomit. Physical examination discloses exquisite abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show elevated serum amylase. Which of the following morphologic changes would be expected in the peripancreatic tissue of this patient?
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis releases lipase from injured acinar cells, which hydrolyzes peripancreatic fat into fatty acids and glycerol; the free fatty acids then bind calcium to form soaps in a process called saponification, producing fat necrosis. This calcium consumption also explains the hypocalcemia often seen after an acute pancreatitis attack. Liquefactive necrosis, while it can occur in severe pancreatitis, is not the classic peripancreatic finding described here. Caseous and fibrinoid necrosis occur in entirely different clinical contexts (granulomatous infection and vasculitis, respectively).
keypoints: ⭐ Saponification = fatty acids + calcium → chalky white soaps visible grossly as peripancreatic fat necrosis
Hypocalcemia is a classic laboratory clue in acute pancreatitis due to calcium consumption during saponification
Elevated serum amylase and lipase are the key diagnostic labs for acute pancreatitis

questions.stem: A CT scan of a 43-year-old woman with a parathyroid adenoma and hyperparathyroidism reveals extensive calcium deposits in the lungs and kidney parenchyma. These radiologic findings are best explained by which of the following mechanisms of disease?
questions.explanation: Metastatic calcification occurs when hypercalcemia (here from a PTH-secreting parathyroid adenoma) drives calcium deposition into otherwise normal tissues, such as the alveolar septa of the lung, renal tubules, and blood vessels. This differs from dystrophic calcification, which occurs in previously damaged tissue despite normal serum calcium levels. Other causes of metastatic calcification include vitamin D excess and osteolytic bone metastases (e.g., from breast cancer). Arteriosclerosis is itself an example of dystrophic calcification, not the correct mechanism here.
keypoints: ⭐ Metastatic calcification = elevated serum calcium + normal tissue; dystrophic calcification = normal serum calcium + damaged tissue
Common causes of hypercalcemia driving metastatic calcification: hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D intoxication, osteolytic bone metastases
Lung and kidney are classic sites for metastatic calcification because of their net alkaline environment favoring calcium salt precipitation

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease dies of congestive heart failure. The brain at autopsy is shown in the image. This patient's brain exemplifies which of the following responses to chronic injury?
questions.explanation: Atrophy is a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue, often from cell loss or shrinkage in response to chronic injury, disuse, or reduced blood supply. In Alzheimer disease, extensive neuronal death causes irreversible cerebral atrophy, grossly visible as thinned gyri and widened sulci, as seen in this specimen. Unlike some forms of atrophy (e.g., disuse atrophy), the neuronal loss here cannot be reversed once cells have died. Anaplasia refers to loss of differentiation in neoplastic cells and does not apply to this degenerative process.
keypoints: ⭐ Alzheimer disease classically shows atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with narrowed gyri and widened sulci
Neurons are permanent (non-dividing) cells, so lost neurons in Alzheimer disease cannot be replaced
Atrophy can be reversible (e.g., disuse atrophy of muscle) or irreversible (e.g., neuronal loss)
questions.imageAlt: Gross specimen of an atrophic brain with widened sulci and thinned gyri
questions.imageCaption: Cerebral atrophy in Alzheimer disease

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of heavy smoking and repeated bouts of pneumonia presents with a 2-week history of fever and productive cough. A chest X-ray reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate. A transbronchial biopsy confirms pneumonia and further demonstrates preneoplastic changes within the bronchial mucosa. Which of the following best characterizes the morphology of this bronchial mucosal lesion?
choices: Increased numbers of otherwise normal cells
Transformation of one differentiated cell type to another
Ulceration and necrosis of epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Dysplasia is characterized by an abnormal pattern of cellular maturation: variation in cell size and shape, nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia, and disorderly arrangement within the epithelium. It is a preneoplastic change commonly induced in bronchial epithelium by carcinogens in tobacco smoke, and it is potentially reversible if the inciting injury (smoking) is removed. Increased numbers of otherwise normal cells describes hyperplasia, not dysplasia, while invasiveness through the basement membrane would indicate frank malignancy rather than a preneoplastic change.
keypoints: ⭐ Dysplasia is preneoplastic but potentially reversible if the causative injury is removed
Bronchial dysplasia progresses along a continuum: metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma
Distinguishing severe dysplasia from carcinoma in situ is a common diagnostic challenge in surgical pathology

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing angina pectoris and arterial hypertension dies of spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage. At autopsy, the heart appears globoid. The left ventricle measures 2.8 cm on cross section (shown in the image). This adaptation to chronic injury was mediated primarily by changes in the intracellular concentration of which of the following components?
questions.explanation: The thickened left ventricular wall represents myocardial hypertrophy, a response to chronic pressure overload from hypertension. Hypertrophy results from increased transcription (increased mRNA), leading to more sarcomeric protein synthesis and larger, but not more numerous, myocytes since cardiac myocytes cannot proliferate. This is mediated by upregulation of growth-promoting genes such as myc, fos, and ras. Increased intracellular water characterizes acute hydropic swelling from sublethal injury, not the chronic adaptive process of hypertrophy.
keypoints: ⭐ Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells; they enlarge (hypertrophy) rather than divide (hyperplasia) in response to increased workload
Hypertrophy is driven by increased expression of protooncogenes (myc, fos, ras) leading to increased mRNA and protein synthesis
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is the classic response to chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension, aortic stenosis)
questions.imageAlt: Gross cross section of a thickened, globoid left ventricle
questions.imageCaption: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with AIDS-dementia complex develops acute pneumonia and dies of respiratory insufficiency. At autopsy, many central nervous system neurons display hydropic degeneration. This manifestation of sublethal neuronal injury was most likely mediated by impairment of which of the following cellular processes?
questions.explanation: Hydropic (cloudy) swelling is a form of sublethal, reversible cell injury caused by failure of cellular volume regulation, chiefly impairment of the plasma membrane sodium pump (Na+/K+-ATPase) or its ATP supply. Sodium accumulates intracellularly, and water follows osmotically, causing the cell and its organelles to swell. Lipid peroxidation is more characteristic of irreversible injury and membrane destruction rather than the initiating event in hydropic swelling. None of the other listed processes directly regulate cell volume.
keypoints: ⭐ Hydropic swelling is the classic light-microscopic hallmark of reversible (sublethal) cell injury
Mechanisms of hydropic swelling: increased membrane Na+ permeability, damaged Na+/K+-ATPase, or ATP depletion
Ultrastructurally, hydropic swelling manifests as dilated endoplasmic reticulum and swollen mitochondria

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man suffers a heart attack and expires. Examination of the lungs at autopsy reveals numerous pigmented nodules scattered throughout the parenchyma (shown in the image). What is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anthracosis is the accumulation of inhaled carbon particles within alveolar macrophages and regional lymph nodes, producing the characteristic black pigmented nodules seen throughout the lung parenchyma. It is extremely common in urban dwellers and smokers and is generally an innocuous finding, in contrast to pneumoconioses such as silicosis or asbestosis, which produce fibrosis and functional impairment from toxic/fibrogenic dusts. Hemosiderosis refers to intracellular iron (hemosiderin) accumulation, which has a golden-brown rather than black appearance, and does not fit this gross description.
keypoints: ⭐ Anthracosis is generally clinically silent; coexisting silica exposure (anthracosilicosis) is what causes pulmonary fibrosis in coal workers
Carbon particles are transported by macrophages to hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, producing visible black nodal pigmentation
Distinguish from asbestosis (ferruginous bodies, lower lobe fibrosis) and silicosis (nodular fibrosis, upper lobes)
questions.imageAlt: Gross lung specimen with numerous black pigmented nodules
questions.imageCaption: Anthracotic pigment deposition throughout lung parenchyma

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus delivers a healthy boy at 38 weeks of gestation. As a result of maternal hyperglycemia during pregnancy, pancreatic islets in the neonate would be expected to show which of the following morphologic responses to injury?
questions.explanation: Chronic fetal exposure to maternal hyperglycemia drives increased insulin demand, and fetal pancreatic beta cells retain proliferative capacity, responding with physiologic hyperplasia. These hyperplastic beta cells can secrete insulin autonomously after delivery (once the maternal glucose supply is cut off), causing neonatal hypoglycemia — a classic complication in infants of diabetic mothers. Metaplasia would imply replacement by a different differentiated cell type, which is not what occurs here; the beta cells simply increase in number.
keypoints: ⭐ Infants of diabetic mothers are at risk for neonatal hypoglycemia due to islet beta-cell hyperplasia and autonomous insulin secretion
Infants of diabetic mothers also have increased risk of macrosomia and congenital anomalies (cardiac, neural tube defects)
Good glycemic control during early gestation reduces the risk of major fetal malformations

questions.stem: A 59-year-old female alcoholic is brought to the emergency room with a fever (38.7°C/103°F) and foul-smelling breath. The patient subsequently develops acute bronchopneumonia and dies of respiratory insufficiency. A pulmonary abscess is identified at autopsy (shown in the image). Histologic examination of the wall of this lesion would most likely demonstrate which of the following pathologic changes?
questions.explanation: Lung abscesses, often from aspiration in alcoholics, form via liquefactive necrosis, in which potent hydrolases released by neutrophils digest dead tissue faster than it can be repaired, producing a pus-filled cavity. This contrasts with coagulative necrosis, in which the cellular outline is initially preserved (as in ischemic infarcts), and caseous necrosis, which is characteristic of necrotizing granulomas such as tuberculosis. Fibrinoid necrosis is a distinct process seen in the walls of blood vessels affected by vasculitis.
keypoints: ⭐ An abscess is, by definition, a localized cavity of liquefactive necrosis filled with pus
The brain is another classic site of liquefactive necrosis (e.g., in cerebral infarcts) due to its high lipid and low collagen content
Foul-smelling breath and aspiration risk in alcoholics predispose to anaerobic lung abscess
questions.imageAlt: Gross lung specimen showing a cavitary pulmonary abscess
questions.imageCaption: Pulmonary abscess with central liquefactive necrosis

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man from China is evaluated for persistent cough, night sweats, low-grade fever, and general malaise. A chest X-ray reveals findings "consistent with a Ghon complex." Sputum cultures grow acid-fast bacilli. Examination of hilar lymph nodes in this patient would most likely demonstrate which of the following pathologic changes?
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis is the hallmark of necrotizing granulomas in primary tuberculosis, producing amorphous, coarsely granular, eosinophilic debris that grossly resembles clumpy cheese. Unlike liquefactive necrosis, caseating debris does not undergo lysis but persists indefinitely, and unlike coagulative necrosis, the underlying cellular architecture is completely obliterated. The Ghon complex refers to the combination of a peripheral parenchymal lung lesion with ipsilateral hilar lymph node involvement, both of which classically show caseous necrosis in primary TB.
keypoints: ⭐ Ghon complex = primary parenchymal TB lesion + caseating hilar lymph node involvement
Caseous necrosis is mediated by the host's cellular immune response (granulomatous inflammation) to mycobacterial antigens, not direct bacterial toxin
Acid-fast staining identifies Mycobacterium tuberculosis due to its waxy, mycolic acid-rich cell wall

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman complains of increased vaginal discharge of 1-month duration. A cervical Pap smear is shown in the image. Superficial epithelial cells are identified with arrows. When compared to cells from the deeper intermediate layer (top), the nuclei of these superficial cells exhibit which of the following cytologic features?
questions.explanation: As squamous epithelial cells mature and migrate toward the surface, their nuclei progressively condense and shrink, a change termed pyknosis, in which chromatin clumps and the nucleus becomes small and deeply basophilic. Karyorrhexis (fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus) and karyolysis (complete dissolution of the nucleus) represent later, more advanced steps in nuclear breakdown that are not features of normal superficial squamous maturation. This question uses normal maturation pyknosis as an analogy to the nuclear changes also seen in coagulative necrosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Sequence of nuclear necrotic changes: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis
Pyknosis in superficial squamous cells is a normal maturation phenomenon, distinct from the pyknosis of necrotic/apoptotic cells
Superficial cells have small, condensed (pyknotic) nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm compared to basophilic intermediate cells
questions.imageAlt: Cervical Pap smear showing superficial squamous cells with arrows indicating pyknotic nuclei
questions.imageCaption: Pap smear demonstrating pyknotic nuclei in superficial squamous cells

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman suffers a tonic-clonic seizure and presents with delirium and hydrophobia. The patient states that she was bitten on the hand by a bat about 1 month ago. The patient subsequently dies of respiratory failure. Viral particles are found throughout the brainstem and cerebellum at autopsy. In addition to direct viral cytotoxicity, the necrosis of virally infected neurons in this patient was mediated primarily by which of the following mechanisms?
choices: Release of oxygen radicals from macrophages
questions.explanation: Both humoral (antibody-mediated) and cellular (cytotoxic T-lymphocyte) arms of the immune system respond to viral antigens presented on infected cell surfaces, eliminating infected neurons via induced apoptosis or complement-mediated cytolysis. This antigen-specific adaptive immune response, rather than nonspecific acute inflammatory mechanisms such as neutrophil phagocytosis or mast cell histamine release, is the dominant driver of neuronal injury in rabies encephalitis. Rabies virus travels by retrograde axoplasmic transport from the peripheral bite wound to the CNS, explaining the brainstem/cerebellar distribution of disease.
keypoints: ⭐ Rabies virus spreads via retrograde axonal transport from the bite site to the CNS, with a typically long incubation period
Negri bodies are classic eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in rabies-infected neurons (especially Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons)
Hydrophobia (fear of water, from painful pharyngeal spasm) is a classic clinical feature of rabies encephalitis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman loses her right kidney following an automobile accident. A CT scan of the abdomen 2 years later shows marked enlargement of the left kidney. The renal enlargement is an example of which of the following adaptations?
questions.explanation: Compensatory enlargement of the remaining kidney after unilateral nephrectomy is termed hypertrophy, reflecting increased organ size and function driven by trophic signals responding to increased physiologic demand. Although some component of renal tubular cell hyperplasia may occur, the overall response is conventionally referred to as hypertrophy in this context, mediated by upregulation of growth-promoting protooncogenes (myc, fos, ras). This is the same fundamental adaptive mechanism as cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.
keypoints: ⭐ Compensatory renal hypertrophy after nephrectomy/nephron loss involves both hypertrophy and some hyperplasia of remaining nephrons
This adaptive response is clinically relevant to living kidney donors, whose remaining kidney compensates over time
Loss of one kidney to trauma or nephrectomy classically results in compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral kidney

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man has profound bleeding from a peptic ulcer and dies of hypovolemic shock. The liver at autopsy displays centrilobular necrosis. Compared to viable hepatocytes, the necrotic cells contain higher intracellular concentrations of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Irreversible cell injury (coagulative necrosis, here from ischemic shock) damages the plasma membrane's ability to maintain the steep calcium gradient normally present between the extracellular space (high calcium) and cytosol (low calcium). This breakdown allows massive calcium influx into the dying cell, activating destructive enzymes (phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases) that further the injury. Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes are especially vulnerable to ischemic injury because they receive the least oxygenated blood and lie farthest from the portal supply. The other listed metals are not characteristically elevated in acutely necrotic cells.
keypoints: ⭐ Calcium influx is a final common pathway of irreversible cell injury, activating phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases
Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes are the most susceptible to hypoxic/ischemic injury ("shock liver")
Normally, extracellular calcium concentration is roughly 10,000-fold higher than intracellular calcium

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is pinned by falling debris during a hurricane. An X-ray film of the leg reveals a compound fracture of the right tibia. The leg is immobilized in a cast for 6 weeks. When the cast is removed, the patient notices that her right leg is weak and visibly smaller in circumference than the left leg. Which of the following terms best describes this change in the patient's leg muscle?
questions.explanation: Prolonged immobilization reduces functional demand on skeletal muscle, leading to disuse atrophy: a reduction in muscle fiber size and repression of differentiation gene expression, with reduced protein synthesis and contractile force. This is a reversible adaptive response — with resumption of activity, atrophic muscle fibers are fully capable of returning to their original size and function. Because the change is a physiologic adaptation to reduced use rather than a vascular insult, ischemic necrosis and irreversible cell injury are incorrect.
keypoints: ⭐ Disuse atrophy is reversible: resumption of normal activity restores muscle fiber size and function
Atrophy in muscle involves decreased protein synthesis and increased protein degradation (via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway)
Cast immobilization is a classic clinical cause of disuse atrophy, distinct from denervation atrophy

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is hospitalized after suffering a mild stroke. While in the hospital, he suddenly develops crushing substernal chest pain. Analysis of serum proteins and ECG confirm a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. The patient subsequently develops an arrhythmia and expires. A cross section of the left ventricle at autopsy is shown in the image. Histologic examination of the affected heart muscle would demonstrate which of the following morphologic changes?
questions.explanation: Ischemic death of cardiac myocytes in myocardial infarction produces coagulative necrosis, in which the basic outline of the dead cell is preserved despite loss of nuclear detail, resembling the coagulation of protein that occurs with heating (hence the name). Interruption of blood supply decreases oxygen and glucose delivery, impairing mitochondrial electron transport, decreasing ATP synthesis, and promoting reactive oxygen species generation and mitochondrial release of cytochrome c. Liquefactive necrosis instead occurs when hydrolytic digestion outpaces repair, as in abscesses or brain infarcts, not in the heart.
keypoints: ⭐ Coagulative necrosis is the characteristic pattern of necrosis in solid organs following ischemic infarction (heart, kidney, spleen)
The brain is a notable exception, undergoing liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis after infarction
Grossly, infarcted myocardium is pale/yellow with a hemorrhagic rim; here it appears pale on cross-section at autopsy
questions.imageAlt: Gross cross section of the left ventricle showing a pale infarcted region
questions.imageCaption: Left ventricular myocardial infarction with coagulative necrosis

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic features would provide definitive evidence of necrosis in the myocardium of the patient described in Question 20?
questions.explanation: Nuclear fragmentation, encompassing karyorrhexis and karyolysis, is a definitive hallmark of coagulative necrosis and irreversible cell death, since these represent complete, irrecoverable breakdown of the nucleus. Disaggregation of polyribosomes, increased intracellular volume, and mitochondrial swelling can all be seen in both reversible (sublethal) and irreversible injury, so they are not diagnostic of necrosis on their own. Lymphocytic infiltration is characteristic of chronic inflammation, not acute ischemic necrosis, which instead recruits neutrophils.
keypoints: ⭐ Nuclear changes of necrosis (in order): pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis, with the latter two being irreversible
Mitochondrial permeability transition (with calcium influx and swelling) is an early trigger of irreversible injury but is not itself definitive proof of cell death
Neutrophils, not lymphocytes, are the dominant infiltrating cell in acute myocardial infarction (peaking around 24-72 hours)

questions.stem: A 90-year-old woman with mild diabetes and Alzheimer disease dies in her sleep. At autopsy, hepatocytes are noted to contain golden cytoplasmic granules that do not stain with Prussian blue. Which of the following best accounts for pigment accumulation in the liver of this patient?
questions.explanation: The golden-brown cytoplasmic granules that do not stain with Prussian blue (ruling out iron/hemosiderin) represent lipofuscin, a "wear-and-tear" pigment that accumulates with advanced age in metabolically active, long-lived cells such as those of the liver, heart, and brain. Lipofuscin consists of peroxidized lipid-protein complexes within lysosomes and simply reflects cumulative oxidative injury over a person's lifetime rather than any specific disease process. Neither Alzheimer disease, congestive heart failure, diabetes, nor hereditary hemochromatosis is the direct cause of lipofuscin accumulation.
keypoints: ⭐ Lipofuscin is the classic "aging pigment": golden-brown, lysosomal, Prussian-blue negative, composed of peroxidized lipids
Distinguish from hemosiderin (iron-containing, Prussian blue positive) and from bilirubin/melanin pigments
Lipofuscin accumulation itself is not thought to be harmful to the cell; it is a marker rather than a cause of aging
questions.imageAlt: Photomicrograph of hepatocytes with golden-brown cytoplasmic lipofuscin granules
questions.imageCaption: Lipofuscin pigment accumulation in hepatocytes

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms of disease best describes the pathogenesis of pigment accumulation in hepatocytes in the patient described in Question 22?
choices: Malabsorption and enhanced deposition of iron
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin forms within lysosomes as a result of ongoing peroxidation of unsaturated fatty acids in cellular membranes, reflecting cumulative oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species that are inadequately neutralized by the cell's antioxidant defenses over time. This process is distinct from iron overload (as in hereditary hemochromatosis) and from melanin or bilirubin metabolism, which are unrelated pigment pathways. As oxidative damage to membranes continues throughout life, lipofuscin progressively accumulates, particularly in long-lived, post-mitotic cells.
keypoints: ⭐ Lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes is the shared mechanism behind both lipofuscin formation and lethal free-radical injury
Antioxidant defenses (glutathione peroxidase, catalase, superoxide dismutase, vitamin E) normally limit this oxidative damage
Lipofuscin is sometimes called "the wear-and-tear pigment" because it accumulates progressively with age

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with increasing abdominal girth and yellow discoloration of his skin and sclera. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly and jaundice. A Prussian blue stain of a liver biopsy is shown in the image. What is the major intracellular iron storage protein in this patient's hepatocytes?
questions.explanation: Hemosiderin is a partially denatured, aggregated form of ferritin that accumulates as yellow-brown cytoplasmic granules and stains blue with the Prussian blue (Perls) reaction, as demonstrated on this biopsy. It is the major storage form of excess iron within hepatocytes, particularly in conditions of iron overload such as hereditary hemochromatosis, where a genetic defect in intestinal iron absorption leads to progressive iron deposition, primarily in the liver. Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein of red blood cells, not the intracellular hepatic storage form, while transferrin is the serum iron-transport protein and bilirubin is unrelated to Prussian blue staining.
keypoints: ⭐ Hemosiderin = denatured, aggregated ferritin; stains positive (blue) with Prussian blue/Perls stain
Hereditary hemochromatosis results from mutations affecting intestinal iron absorption (commonly HFE gene), causing progressive multi-organ iron deposition
Iron overload classically causes a triad of cirrhosis, diabetes ("bronze diabetes"), and skin pigmentation
questions.imageAlt: Prussian blue stained liver biopsy showing blue-staining iron deposits in hepatocytes
questions.imageCaption: Prussian blue stain highlighting hemosiderin (iron) accumulation in hepatocytes

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic cystitis complains of urinary frequency and pelvic discomfort. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable. Biopsy of the bladder mucosa reveals foci of glandular epithelium and chronic inflammatory cells. No cytologic signs of atypia or malignancy are observed. Which of the following terms best describes the morphologic response to chronic injury in this patient?
questions.explanation: Metaplasia is the replacement of one differentiated cell type by another differentiated cell type, and here the normal transitional epithelium of the bladder is replaced by glandular epithelium in the setting of chronic inflammation (cystitis glandularis). This is considered a protective adaptive response to persistent irritation, though it is not always harmless — metaplastic epithelium can occasionally serve as a substrate for neoplastic transformation. The absence of cytologic atypia rules out dysplasia, which would show disordered maturation and nuclear abnormalities.
keypoints: ⭐ Cystitis glandularis: metaplasia of transitional (urothelial) epithelium to glandular epithelium from chronic bladder irritation/inflammation
Squamous metaplasia of the bronchus in smokers is the classic parallel example of protective but imperfect metaplasia
Metaplastic tissue retains some malignant potential and warrants surveillance in high-risk settings

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of hyperlipidemia dies of cardiac arrhythmia following a massive heart attack. Peroxidation of which of the following molecules was primarily responsible for causing the loss of membrane integrity in cardiac myocytes in this patient?
questions.explanation: During oxidative injury, hydroxyl radicals abstract a hydrogen atom from the unsaturated fatty acid chains of membrane phospholipids, generating a lipid radical that reacts with molecular oxygen to form a lipid peroxide radical; this initiates a self-propagating chain reaction that degrades phospholipids into smaller fragments and destroys the structural integrity of the plasma and organelle membranes. Proteins (such as sodium-potassium ATPase) are also targets of reactive oxygen species, but protein cross-linking does not cause the same rapid loss of membrane integrity as phospholipid peroxidation. This mechanism is central to reperfusion injury following myocardial infarction.
keypoints: ⭐ Lipid peroxidation is a self-propagating free-radical chain reaction that destroys the unsaturated fatty acids of membrane phospholipids
Membrane damage from lipid peroxidation leads to loss of ionic gradients, calcium influx, and ultimately cell death
Reactive oxygen species generated during ischemia-reperfusion are a major contributor to this process after MI

questions.stem: A 22-year-old construction worker sticks himself with a sharp, rusty nail. Within 24 hours, the wound has enlarged to become a 1-cm sore that drains thick, purulent material. This skin wound illustrates which of the following morphologic types of necrosis?
questions.explanation: The formation of thick, purulent (pus-filled) drainage reflects liquefactive necrosis, in which neutrophils recruited to the site of bacterial infection release potent hydrolytic enzymes that digest dead tissue, creating a localized abscess. This is the same basic process seen in pulmonary abscesses and represents rapid dissolution of tissue rather than the preserved cellular architecture of coagulative necrosis. Caseous and fibrinoid necrosis occur in entirely different clinical settings (granulomatous infection and vasculitis, respectively) and would not present as a purulent draining skin wound.
keypoints: ⭐ Pus formation is the clinical hallmark of liquefactive necrosis driven by neutrophil-derived hydrolases
Puncture wounds with organic/rusty material carry a risk of Clostridium tetani infection, warranting tetanus prophylaxis
Acute inflammation (neutrophilic infiltrate) is the driving process behind abscess/liquefactive necrosis formation

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man undergoes liver biopsy for evaluation of the grade and stage of his hepatitis C virus infection. The biopsy reveals swollen (ballooned) hepatocytes and moderate lobular inflammatory activity (shown in the image). The arrow identifies an acidophilic (Councilman) body. Which of the following cellular processes best accounts for the presence of scattered acidophilic bodies in this liver biopsy?
questions.explanation: Acidophilic (Councilman) bodies are deeply eosinophilic, membrane-bound remnants of individual hepatocytes that have undergone apoptosis, a programmed, self-directed pathway of cell death triggered by both extracellular and intracellular signals, including viral infection. These extruded apoptotic remnants are visible by light microscopy as discrete round eosinophilic structures within the sinusoids, distinct from the confluent zonal necrosis of coagulative necrosis. Apoptosis serves as a defense mechanism that eliminates individual infected or damaged hepatocytes in chronic viral hepatitis without eliciting the same degree of surrounding inflammation as necrosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Councilman (acidophilic) bodies = apoptotic hepatocytes, classically seen in viral hepatitis (and yellow fever)
Apoptosis is energy (ATP)-dependent and does not provoke the inflammatory response typical of necrosis
Apoptosis affects single scattered cells, whereas necrosis typically affects contiguous groups of cells
questions.imageAlt: Liver biopsy with an arrow pointing to an eosinophilic Councilman (apoptotic) body
questions.imageCaption: Liver biopsy in hepatitis C showing a Councilman body

questions.stem: Which of the following biochemical changes characterizes the formation of acidophilic bodies in the patient described in Question 29?
choices: Loss of tumor suppressor protein p53
questions.explanation: Fragmentation of chromosomal DNA at internucleosomal sites by activated endonucleases is a defining biochemical feature of apoptosis, producing the characteristic "laddering" pattern seen on gel electrophoresis (in contrast to the random DNA smearing seen in necrosis). While DNA fragmentation can also occur in necrosis, only apoptosis produces the regular, nucleosome-length banding pattern used as a distinguishing laboratory marker. Mitochondrial swelling is a nonspecific feature of both reversible and irreversible cell injury and is not a distinctive marker of programmed cell death.
keypoints: ⭐ Apoptotic DNA fragmentation produces a characteristic "laddering" pattern on gel electrophoresis (multiples of ~180-200 bp nucleosome units)
Endonuclease-mediated cleavage occurs at internucleosomal linker DNA, sparing DNA wrapped around histones
p53 often triggers, rather than is lost during, the apoptotic response to DNA damage

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with a history of hyperlipidemia and hypertension develops progressive, right renal artery stenosis. Over time, this patient's right kidney is likely to demonstrate which of the following morphologic adaptations to partial ischemia?
questions.explanation: Partial ischemia, as occurs with incomplete occlusion from renal artery stenosis or inadequate collateral circulation, produces a chronic reduction in oxygen delivery that is compatible with continued cell viability but leads to cell atrophy over time as the tissue "scales back" its metabolic demands. This is distinct from total ischemia, which causes outright cell death (infarction). Atrophy from chronic partial ischemia is also classically seen at the margins of infarcts in the heart, brain, and kidney.
keypoints: ⭐ Partial/chronic ischemia → atrophy; total/acute ischemia → necrosis/infarction
Renal artery stenosis is an important, potentially reversible cause of secondary hypertension
Chronically atrophic but viable kidney tissue may partially recover function if blood flow is restored (revascularization)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy suffers blunt trauma to the leg in an automobile accident. Six months later, bone trabeculae have formed within the striated skeletal muscle at the site of tissue injury. This pathologic condition is an example of which of the following morphologic adaptations to injury?
questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans is characterized by the formation of true bony trabeculae within injured skeletal muscle, representing osseous metaplasia — the replacement of one normal differentiated tissue type (muscle) by another normal differentiated tissue type (bone) in response to injury. This differs from dystrophic calcification, which involves deposition of amorphous calcium salts in damaged tissue but does not produce organized bone trabeculae. Because serum calcium is normal in this scenario and the change is localized to the injury site, metastatic calcification is also incorrect.
keypoints: ⭐ Myositis ossificans = heterotopic bone formation within muscle following trauma, an example of osseous metaplasia
Unlike dystrophic calcification, myositis ossificans produces organized trabecular bone, not amorphous calcium deposits
Myositis ossificans can mimic a bone-forming sarcoma radiographically and histologically, causing diagnostic confusion

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presents with a scaly, erythematous lesion on the dorsal surface of his left hand. A skin biopsy reveals atypical keratinocytes filling the entire thickness of the epidermis (shown in the image). The arrows point to apoptotic bodies. Which of the following proteins plays the most important role in mediating programmed cell death in this patient's skin cancer?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c release from mitochondria is a pivotal event in the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis: once released into the cytosol, cytochrome c activates Apaf-1, converting procaspase-9 to active caspase-9, which then activates downstream effector caspases that cleave nuclear and cytoskeletal proteins to execute the morphologic and biochemical changes of apoptosis. Catalase and superoxide dismutase are antioxidant enzymes that neutralize reactive oxygen species (which can trigger apoptosis) but do not themselves mediate the apoptotic execution pathway. Myeloperoxidase is a neutrophil enzyme unrelated to programmed cell death.
keypoints: ⭐ Mitochondrial cytochrome c release → Apaf-1 activation → procaspase-9 → caspase-9 → downstream effector caspases is the core intrinsic apoptotic pathway
This lesion (full-thickness epidermal atypia) describes squamous cell carcinoma in situ / invasive SCC
Effector caspases cleave nuclear lamins, cytoskeletal proteins, and activate endonucleases responsible for apoptotic morphology
questions.imageAlt: Skin biopsy with arrows pointing to apoptotic bodies within atypical epidermis
questions.imageCaption: Squamous cell carcinoma with apoptotic bodies

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with a history of suicidal depression swallows a commercial solvent. A liver biopsy is performed to assess the degree of damage to the hepatic parenchyma. Histologic examination demonstrates severe swelling of the centrilobular hepatocytes (shown in the image). Which of the following mechanisms of disease best accounts for the reversible changes noted in this liver biopsy?
choices: Increased storage of triglycerides and free fatty acids
Protein aggregation due to increased cytosolic pH
questions.explanation: The swollen (ballooned) hepatocytes seen here represent hydropic swelling, a reversible form of sublethal cell injury that occurs when a toxin depletes intracellular ATP stores, impairing the plasma membrane Na+/K+-ATPase pump. Sodium then accumulates within the cell, and water follows osmotically, causing generalized cellular and organelle swelling. Because this depends on ATP depletion rather than lysosomal rupture or mitochondrial permeability transition (which mark irreversible injury), the process remains reversible if the toxin is removed and ATP synthesis is restored.
keypoints: ⭐ Hydropic swelling is reversible; it precedes and can progress to irreversible injury if ATP depletion is severe/prolonged
Solvent hepatotoxins are often bioactivated by cytochrome P450 (mixed function oxidase system) in the smooth ER
Lysosomal membrane rupture and mitochondrial permeability transition mark the transition to irreversible cell injury
questions.imageAlt: Liver biopsy showing severely swollen, ballooned centrilobular hepatocytes
questions.imageCaption: Hydropic swelling of centrilobular hepatocytes following solvent toxicity

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is pulled from the ocean after a boating accident and resuscitated. Six hours later, the patient develops acute renal failure. Kidney biopsy reveals evidence of karyorrhexis and karyolysis in renal tubular epithelial cells. Which of the following biochemical events preceded these pathologic changes?
questions.explanation: During ischemia, lack of oxygen halts oxidative phosphorylation, forcing cells into anaerobic glycolysis, which generates excess lactate and lowers intracellular pH. This progressive intracellular acidification initiates a cascade of enzymatic and structural derangements that propels the cell toward irreversible injury and necrosis (here manifesting as acute tubular necrosis with karyorrhexis and karyolysis). The other listed choices describe changes in the opposite direction of what actually occurs during ischemic injury — ATP production falls rather than rises, and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump fails rather than activates.
keypoints: ⭐ Ischemia → anaerobic glycolysis → lactate accumulation → intracellular acidosis is an early step preceding irreversible injury
Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is a classic cause of acute kidney injury following hypotension/shock ("near-drowning" ischemic insult)
Karyorrhexis and karyolysis represent later, irreversible steps in nuclear breakdown beyond initial pyknosis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with symptoms of acute renal failure. His blood pressure is 220/130 mm Hg (malignant hypertension). While in the emergency room, the patient suffers a stroke and expires. Microscopic examination of the kidney at autopsy is shown in the image. Which of the following morphologic changes accounts for the red material in the wall of the artery?
questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis is an alteration of injured blood vessel walls in which insudation and accumulation of plasma proteins (including fibrin) cause the vessel wall to stain intensely eosinophilic (red) with hematoxylin and eosin, as seen here. It is characteristic of malignant hypertension, in which extremely high blood pressures damage the endothelium and allow plasma protein leakage into the vessel wall, and is also seen in necrotizing vasculitides. This differs fundamentally from the other necrosis subtypes, which affect parenchymal tissue rather than vessel walls.
keypoints: ⭐ Fibrinoid necrosis is specific to blood vessel walls, seen classically in malignant hypertension and necrotizing vasculitis
Malignant hypertension (diastolic often >120-130 mm Hg) is a hypertensive emergency that can cause acute renal failure and encephalopathy
"Onion-skin" hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is another characteristic renal vascular lesion seen in malignant hypertension
questions.imageAlt: Photomicrograph of a renal artery wall with bright pink/red fibrinoid material
questions.imageCaption: Fibrinoid necrosis of a renal artery wall in malignant hypertension

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman develops an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency) 3 months after suffering massive hemorrhage during the delivery of her baby. A CT scan of the abdomen shows small adrenal glands. Which of the following mechanisms of disease best accounts for adrenal atrophy in this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient has Sheehan syndrome: postpartum hemorrhage causes ischemic infarction of the anterior pituitary, resulting in decreased ACTH (corticotropin) secretion. Because the adrenal cortex depends on ACTH as a trophic (growth-maintaining) signal, its loss leads to progressive adrenal cortical atrophy and subsequent adrenal insufficiency, manifesting later as an Addisonian crisis. This is a classic example of atrophy from loss of trophic hormonal stimulation rather than from direct ischemia, inflammation, or infection of the adrenal gland itself.
keypoints: ⭐ Sheehan syndrome: postpartum hemorrhage/hypotension → pituitary ischemic necrosis → panhypopituitarism (including ACTH deficiency)
Secondary adrenal insufficiency (ACTH deficiency) differs from primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) in that hyperpigmentation is absent (ACTH-related MSH effect is lost, not gained)
Tuberculosis and hemorrhagic necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) are causes of primary, not secondary, adrenal insufficiency

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking complains of chronic cough. A "coin lesion" is discovered in his right upper lobe on chest X-ray. Bronchoscopy and biopsy fail to identify a mass, but the bronchial mucosa displays squamous metaplasia. What is the most likely outcome of this morphologic adaptation if the patient stops smoking?
questions.explanation: Metaplasia is almost always a response to persistent injury and is, in most cases, a fully reversible adaptive mechanism. Bronchial squamous metaplasia results from prolonged tobacco smoke exposure; when the causative injury (smoking) is removed, the metaplastic epithelium typically reverts to its normal ciliated columnar phenotype over time. This reversibility distinguishes metaplasia from both malignant transformation and necrosis with scarring, which represent irreversible endpoints rather than adaptive, reversible changes.
keypoints: ⭐ Metaplasia is generally reversible upon removal of the inciting stimulus, unlike dysplasia (which may persist/progress) or carcinoma
Squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium impairs normal mucociliary clearance, itself a maladaptive tradeoff
Continued smoking risks progression along the sequence: metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma

questions.stem: A 60-year-old farmer presents with multiple patches of discoloration on his face. Biopsy of lesional skin reveals actinic keratosis. Which of the following terms best describes this response of the skin to chronic sunlight exposure?
questions.explanation: Actinic keratosis is a dysplastic lesion of sun-damaged skin, composed of atypical squamous keratinocytes that vary in size and shape and fail to show the normal orderly maturation pattern as cells progress from the basal layer to the surface. Dysplasia is a preneoplastic change — a necessary stage in the multistep progression toward cancer — but unlike frank carcinoma, dysplastic cells are not fully autonomous, and the tissue can potentially revert toward normal if the inciting injury (chronic UV exposure) is reduced. None of the other adaptive responses (atrophy, hyperplasia, hypertrophy, metaplasia) describe this atypical, disordered maturation pattern.
keypoints: ⭐ Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma if untreated
Chronic UV exposure causes direct DNA damage (pyrimidine dimers) driving keratinocyte dysplasia
Actinic keratosis classically appears as rough, scaly, erythematous patches on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, dorsal hands)

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman smoker complains of intermittent blood in her urine. Urinalysis confirms 4+ hematuria. A CBC reveals increased red cell mass (hematocrit). A CT scan demonstrates a 3-cm renal mass, and a CT-guided biopsy displays renal cell carcinoma. Which of the following cellular adaptations in the bone marrow best explains the increased hematocrit in this patient?
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinomas frequently secrete ectopic erythropoietin, which stimulates proliferation and survival of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, producing erythroid hyperplasia and a secondary, paraneoplastic polycythemia (elevated hematocrit). This mirrors the physiologic hyperplasia seen with appropriately elevated erythropoietin at high altitude, but here the stimulus is inappropriate tumor-derived hormone secretion. None of the other adaptive responses account for an increase in circulating red cell mass, since hyperplasia specifically denotes an increase in cell number.
keypoints: ⭐ Renal cell carcinoma is a classic cause of paraneoplastic erythrocytosis via ectopic erythropoietin secretion
Other paraneoplastic syndromes associated with RCC include hypercalcemia (PTHrP) and Stauffer syndrome (nonmetastatic hepatic dysfunction)
Painless hematuria plus a renal mass in an older smoker is the classic presentation of renal cell carcinoma

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has an abnormal cervical Pap smear. A cervical biopsy reveals that the epithelium lacks normal polarity (shown in the image). Individual cells display hyperchromatic nuclei, a larger nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, and disorderly tissue arrangement. Which of the following adaptations to chronic injury best describes these changes in the patient's cervical epithelium?
questions.explanation: Dysplasia is defined by disordered growth and maturation of an epithelium: variation in cell size and shape, nuclear hyperchromasia with an increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, and loss of the normal orderly polarity of the tissue, exactly as described in this cervical biopsy. Dysplasia is thought to arise from an accumulating series of mutations in a proliferating cell population, and severe dysplasia can be difficult to distinguish histologically from early (in situ) carcinoma. This is the classic pattern of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), a well-recognized precursor to invasive cervical cancer, typically driven by high-risk HPV infection.
keypoints: ⭐ Cervical dysplasia (CIN) is a precursor lesion to invasive cervical squamous cell carcinoma, most often driven by high-risk HPV (16, 18)
Loss of tissue polarity plus hyperchromatic, enlarged nuclei is the defining histologic triad of dysplasia
Distinguishing severe dysplasia from carcinoma in situ is a well-known diagnostic challenge for pathologists
questions.imageAlt: Cervical biopsy showing disorganized dysplastic epithelium with hyperchromatic nuclei
questions.imageCaption: Cervical dysplasia (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of fatigue, mild fever, and an erythematous scaling rash. She also notes joint pain and swelling, primarily involving the small bones of her fingers. Physical examination reveals erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scales that induce punctate bleeding points when removed. Biopsy of lesional skin reveals markedly increased thickness of the epidermis (shown in the image). Which of the following terms best describes this adaptation to chronic injury in this patient with psoriasis?
questions.explanation: Psoriasis is characterized by persistent epidermal hyperplasia, an increase in the number of otherwise normal-appearing keratinocytes resulting from deregulated epidermal proliferation and abnormal signaling, along with altered dermal microcirculation. This produces the markedly thickened epidermis seen on biopsy and the classic silvery, scaling plaques that bleed in a punctate fashion when removed (Auspitz sign) due to the thinned suprapapillary epidermis and dilated dermal capillaries. Unlike dysplasia, psoriatic keratinocytes are cytologically normal and simply increased in number, without atypia or disordered maturation.
keypoints: ⭐ Auspitz sign (punctate bleeding when scale is removed) reflects thinned suprapapillary epidermis over dilated dermal papillary capillaries
Psoriatic arthritis (as described here, involving finger DIP joints) occurs in a subset of psoriasis patients
Psoriasis involves T-cell-mediated immune dysregulation driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation (Th17 pathway)
questions.imageAlt: Skin biopsy showing markedly thickened, hyperplastic epidermis in psoriasis
questions.imageCaption: Epidermal hyperplasia in psoriasis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of fatigue and recurrent fever. She also complains of tenderness below the right costal margin and dark urine. Physical examination reveals jaundice and mild hepatomegaly. The serum is positive for hepatitis B virus antigen. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of indirect virus-mediated hepatocyte cell death in this patient?
choices: Immune recognition of viral antigens on the cell surface
Impaired plasma membrane Na+/K+ ATPase activity
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus is generally noncytopathic; hepatocyte injury in chronic HBV infection is predominantly mediated indirectly through the host immune response, in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize viral antigens presented on the infected hepatocyte surface (in the context of MHC class I) and eliminate the cell, either by inducing apoptosis or via complement-mediated lysis triggered by antiviral antibodies. This immune-mediated mechanism contrasts with direct viral cytotoxicity, where the virus itself disrupts cellular metabolism or membrane integrity (as with some other hepatotoxic viruses).
keypoints: ⭐ HBV itself is largely noncytopathic; liver injury results mainly from the host's own cytotoxic T-cell response to infected hepatocytes
This immune-mediated injury explains why immunosuppressed patients may have higher viral loads but less liver damage
Chronic HBV infection carries increased long-term risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a history of radiation/bone marrow transplantation for leukemia presents with severe diarrhea. He subsequently develops septic shock and expires. Microscopic examination of the colon epithelium at autopsy reveals numerous acidophilic bodies and small cells with pyknotic nuclei. Which of the following proteins most likely played a key role in triggering radiation-induced cell death in this patient's colonic mucosa?
questions.explanation: p53 is the key tumor suppressor protein that senses genomic damage, such as that inflicted by ionizing radiation, and determines whether the cell can repair the damage or must undergo apoptosis. When DNA damage is irreparable, p53 downregulates the antiapoptotic protein Bcl-2 while upregulating proapoptotic genes such as bax and bak, driving the cell into programmed death — explaining the acidophilic bodies and pyknotic nuclei seen in this radiation-injured colonic epithelium. The other listed proteins (cytochrome P450, β-catenin, E-cadherin, P-selectin) play roles in drug metabolism, cell adhesion, or leukocyte trafficking, but are not central mediators of the DNA damage response leading to apoptosis.
keypoints: ⭐ p53 ("guardian of the genome") arrests cells in G1 to allow DNA repair, or triggers apoptosis via bax/bak upregulation and Bcl-2 downregulation if damage is irreparable
Rapidly dividing tissues (bone marrow, GI epithelium, hair follicles) are especially radiosensitive, explaining this patient's severe diarrhea and mucosal injury
Radiation-induced GI mucosal injury ("radiation enteritis") can progress to sepsis from loss of the epithelial barrier, as seen in this fatal case

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman nursing her newborn develops a tender erythematous area around the nipple of her left breast. A thick, yellow fluid is observed to drain from an open fissure. Examination of this breast fluid under the light microscope will most likely reveal an abundance of which of the following inflammatory cells?
questions.explanation: The thick, yellow drainage described is a purulent exudate, the hallmark of acute pyogenic bacterial infection (acute mastitis). The dominant cell type in purulent exudates is the segmented neutrophil (PMN), which is rapidly recruited to sites of bacterial invasion. Mast cells are granulated IgE-bearing cells that release vasoactive mediators in allergic reactions, not purulent infections. B lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate chronic, antigen-specific immunity and predominate in chronic rather than acute inflammation.
keypoints: ⭐ Purulent (suppurative) exudate = pus = neutrophils + liquefied necrotic debris
Acute mastitis is most common in breastfeeding women, typically due to Staphylococcus aureus entering through a cracked nipple
Neutrophils are short-lived cells recruited within hours via chemotactic gradients (C5a, LTB4, IL-8)

questions.stem: Which of the following mediators of inflammation facilitates chemotaxis, cytolysis, and opsonization at the site of inflammation in the patient described in Question 1?
questions.explanation: Complement activation generates fragments and complexes (C5a, C3b, C5b-9) that together mediate all three named functions: C5a is a potent chemotactic factor, C3b acts as an opsonin, and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex causes cytolysis. Kinins mediate pain and vascular permeability but have no direct opsonizing or cytolytic activity. None of the other listed mediators combine chemotaxis, cytolysis, and opsonization in one molecule family.
keypoints: ⭐ C3b and C4b are the principal opsonins of the complement system
C5a also triggers mast cell degranulation (anaphylatoxin activity), distinct from its chemotactic role
The membrane attack complex (C5b-9) forms pores in the lipid bilayer, causing osmotic lysis

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man suffers a massive heart attack and expires 24 hours later due to ventricular arrhythmia. Histologic examination of the affected heart muscle at autopsy would show an abundance of which of the following inflammatory cells?
questions.explanation: By 24 hours after coronary occlusion, neutrophils have marginated, adhered, and transmigrated into the infarcted myocardium to begin debriding necrotic tissue. Neutrophils are the dominant cell of acute inflammation in the first 1-3 days post-infarct, whereas macrophages become prominent around day 3-7 to clear debris and orchestrate repair. Lymphocytes and plasma cells are effectors of chronic, antigen-driven inflammation and are not featured in this early time frame.
keypoints: ⭐ Timeline of MI histology: neutrophils (1-3 days) → macrophages (3-7 days) → granulation tissue (1-2 weeks) → collagenous scar (weeks-months)
Coagulative necrosis is visible by light microscopy as early as 4-12 hours (nuclear pyknosis, hypereosinophilic cytoplasm)
Ventricular arrhythmia in the first 24-48 hours is the leading cause of sudden death after acute MI, often before extensive scarring occurs

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy punctures his thumb with a rusty nail. Four hours later, the thumb appears red and swollen. Initial swelling of the boy's thumb is primarily due to which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammatory edema results primarily from increased permeability of the endothelial barrier, which allows protein-rich fluid to leak into the interstitium (an exudate). This differs from noninflammatory edema, which results from altered Starling forces (hydrostatic/oncotic pressure changes) without endothelial injury. Acute inflammation does not change plasma oncotic pressure, so choices involving oncotic pressure are incorrect, and arteriolar vasodilation (not vasoconstriction) is the vascular event that accompanies acute inflammation.
keypoints: ⭐ Vasodilation of arterioles increases blood flow (hyperemia); it is venular endothelial gap formation that drives fluid leakage
Histamine and bradykinin are classic early mediators of increased vascular permeability via endothelial cell contraction
Exudate (protein-rich, inflammatory) is distinguished from transudate (protein-poor, hemodynamic) by fluid protein content

questions.stem: Which of the following serum proteins activates the complement, coagulation, and fibrinolytic systems at the site of injury in the patient described in Question 5?
questions.explanation: Hageman factor (clotting factor XII) is the central plasma protein that, once activated by contact with exposed subendothelial collagen, simultaneously triggers the coagulation cascade, the fibrinolytic system (via plasminogen to plasmin), the kinin system (via prekallikrein to kallikrein), and the alternative complement pathway. The other choices are each downstream products of Hageman factor activation with narrower functions (e.g., kallikrein generates kinins; plasmin lyses fibrin). This convergence explains why severe tissue trauma often triggers coordinated activation of multiple plasma protein cascades.
keypoints: ⭐ Hageman factor (factor XII) is the classic 'master switch' linking coagulation, fibrinolysis, kinin, and complement systems
Deficiency of factor XII paradoxically causes a prolonged aPTT without a bleeding tendency
Kallikrein converts kininogen to bradykinin, mediating pain and vascular permeability

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with a 4-hour history of fever, shaking chills, and disorientation. Her blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diffuse purpura on her upper arms and chest. Blood cultures are positive for Gram-negative organisms. Which of the following cytokines is primarily involved in the pathogenesis of direct vascular injury in this patient with septic shock?
questions.explanation: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) from Gram-negative bacteria stimulates monocytes/macrophages to release large amounts of TNF-α, which causes direct cytotoxic injury to capillary endothelial cells, contributing to the vascular leak, hypotension, and purpura seen in septic shock. IL-1 also contributes to systemic inflammatory responses (fever, acute phase reaction) but is less directly cytotoxic to endothelium than TNF-α. IFN-γ, PDGF, and TGF-β are not primary mediators of endotoxin-induced vascular injury.
keypoints: ⭐ TNF-α and IL-1 together drive fever, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation in septic shock
High-dose TNF-α causes disseminated intravascular thrombosis and hemorrhagic necrosis (originally described as 'cachectin')
Endotoxin binds CD14/TLR4 on macrophages to trigger this cytokine cascade

questions.stem: A 24-year-old intravenous drug abuser develops a 2-day history of severe headache and fever. His temperature is 38.7°C (103°F). Blood cultures are positive for Gram-positive cocci. The patient is given intravenous antibiotics, but he deteriorates rapidly and dies. A cross section of the brain at autopsy (shown in the image) reveals two encapsulated cavities. Which of the following terms best characterizes this pathologic finding?
questions.explanation: The encapsulated, pus-filled cavities represent cerebral abscesses — the classic example of suppurative (purulent) inflammation, which combines a neutrophilic purulent exudate with significant liquefactive necrosis, here walled off by a rim of granulation tissue. Bacteremia from IV drug use is a well-known route of hematogenous seeding of brain abscesses, often with Gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. Granulomatous inflammation (choice C) is the response to indigestible or slow-growing pathogens like mycobacteria, not pyogenic bacteria, and reactive gliosis is a nonspecific glial response not itself visible grossly as a cavity.
keypoints: ⭐ Brain abscesses form a central purulent cavity surrounded by a fibrous/granulation tissue capsule
IV drug users are at increased risk for right-sided endocarditis and hematogenous seeding of distant organs, including brain and lung
Unlike other organs, brain abscesses cause significant mass effect and can be rapidly fatal from herniation
questions.imageAlt: Gross cross section of brain showing two encapsulated cavities (cerebral abscesses)
questions.imageCaption: Cerebral abscesses with central purulent cavities from hematogenous seeding

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with pneumococcal pneumonia develops a right pleural effusion. The pleural fluid displays a high specific gravity and contains large numbers of polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocytes. Which of the following best characterizes this pleural effusion?
questions.explanation: A pleural effusion with high specific gravity (indicating high protein content) and abundant PMNs is a purulent exudate — the fluid analog of pus, seen in complicated parapneumonic effusions and empyema. A transudate has low protein/specific gravity and lacks a cellular response, reflecting hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance rather than infection. Fibrinous exudate is rich in fibrin but not defined by a prominent PMN infiltrate, and serosanguineous exudate contains red blood cells, giving it a red tinge, which is not described here.
keypoints: ⭐ Light's criteria distinguish exudative from transudative effusions using pleural fluid/serum protein and LDH ratios
Untreated purulent parapneumonic effusion can progress to empyema requiring chest tube drainage
High specific gravity of pleural fluid correlates with high protein content, the biochemical hallmark of an exudate

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presents with a 5-week history of calf pain and swelling and low-grade fever. Serum levels of creatine kinase are elevated. A muscle biopsy reveals numerous eosinophils. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's myalgia?
questions.explanation: Eosinophilic infiltration of skeletal muscle strongly suggests parasitic infestation, classically Trichinella spiralis, which encysts within striated muscle and provokes a marked eosinophilic response along with elevated creatine kinase from myofiber damage. Bacterial infections recruit neutrophils, viral infections recruit lymphocytes, and although muscular dystrophy also elevates CK, it does not produce an eosinophil-rich infiltrate. Autoimmune myositis (e.g., polymyositis) is typically lymphocyte-predominant, not eosinophil-predominant.
keypoints: ⭐ Trichinosis is acquired from undercooked pork or wild game containing encysted Trichinella larvae
Peripheral eosinophilia and periorbital edema are additional classic clues to trichinosis
Eosinophils release major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein, which are toxic to helminths (and surrounding host tissue)

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with a history of recurrent bacterial infections presents with fever and a productive cough. Biochemical analysis of his neutrophils demonstrates that he has an impaired ability to generate reactive oxygen species. This patient most likely has inherited mutations in the gene that encodes which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease results from inherited defects in NADPH oxidase, the enzyme complex responsible for the neutrophil respiratory burst that generates superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide, the substrates for microbial killing. Without this oxidative machinery, phagocytes cannot efficiently kill catalase-positive organisms, leading to recurrent infections and granuloma formation. Myeloperoxidase deficiency (choice C) impairs conversion of H2O2 to hypochlorous acid but does not eliminate reactive oxygen species generation altogether, and it selectively increases susceptibility to Candida rather than a broad range of bacteria.
keypoints: ⭐ CGD patients are classically susceptible to catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia)
The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test or dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay is used to diagnose CGD
X-linked CGD (gp91phox mutation) is the most common inheritance pattern

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man complains of a 2-week history of increasing abdominal pain and yellow discoloration of his sclera. Physical examination reveals right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory studies show elevated serum levels of alkaline phosphatase (520 U/dL) and bilirubin (3.0 mg/dL). A liver biopsy shows portal fibrosis, with scattered foreign bodies consistent with schistosome eggs. Which of the following inflammatory cells is most likely to predominate in the portal tracts in the liver of this patient?
questions.explanation: Schistosome eggs deposited in portal tracts elicit a marked eosinophilic granulomatous reaction, as eosinophils are the principal effector cells against helminthic parasites and their ova. This chronic egg-induced inflammation drives progressive periportal ('pipestem') fibrosis and can lead to portal hypertension. Plasma cells and macrophages participate in chronic inflammation generally but are not the predominant, defining cell type in schistosomal egg granulomas, and basophils/monocytes are not characteristically featured.
keypoints: ⭐ Schistosoma mansoni and S. japonicum classically cause periportal ('pipestem') hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension
Eosinophils contain major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein that are directly toxic to helminth larvae
Chronic schistosomiasis of the bladder (S. haematobium) is associated with squamous cell carcinoma

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman complains of excessive menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain of 4 months. She uses an intrauterine device for contraception. Endometrial biopsy (shown in the image) reveals an excess of plasma cells (arrows) and macrophages within the stroma. The presence of these cells and scattered lymphoid follicles within the endometrial stroma is evidence of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Plasma cells, macrophages, and lymphoid follicles within the endometrial stroma are the histologic hallmark of chronic endometritis, often precipitated by a foreign body such as an IUD or retained products of conception. Acute inflammation is characterized instead by neutrophils, and normal menstrual endometrium does not show this chronic, antibody-producing cellular infiltrate. Granulomatous inflammation would show epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, which are not described here.
keypoints: ⭐ Plasma cells are the single most specific marker of chronic endometritis on biopsy (normal endometrial stroma lacks plasma cells)
IUDs, retained products of conception, and pelvic inflammatory disease are common causes of chronic endometritis
Chronic endometritis is a recognized contributor to abnormal uterine bleeding and infertility
questions.imageAlt: Endometrial biopsy showing plasma cells (arrows) and macrophages within the stroma
questions.imageCaption: Chronic endometritis with plasma cell infiltrate

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer presents with a 3-day history of fever and chest pain. Cardiac catheterization reveals a markedly reduced ejection fraction with normal coronary blood flow. A myocardial biopsy is obtained, and a PCR test for coxsackievirus is positive. Histologic examination of this patient's myocardium will most likely reveal an abundance of which of the following inflammatory cells?
questions.explanation: Viral myocarditis is characterized by lymphocytic infiltration, since naïve T and B lymphocytes are activated by antigen-presenting cells in lymphoid organs and subsequently recruited to peripheral tissue infected by virus, such as the heart. Coxsackievirus B is the classic cause of viral myocarditis and can produce a dilated cardiomyopathy-like picture with reduced ejection fraction despite patent coronary arteries. Neutrophils dominate acute pyogenic or ischemic injury rather than viral infection, and eosinophils/mast cells are not typical of this process.
keypoints: ⭐ Coxsackievirus B is the most common cause of viral myocarditis, which can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy
Normal coronary angiography with reduced EF and fever should prompt consideration of myocarditis over ischemic cardiomyopathy
Endomyocardial biopsy with lymphocytic infiltrate and myocyte necrosis (Dallas criteria) confirms the diagnosis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and hypertension develops end-stage renal disease and dies in uremia. A shaggy fibrin-rich exudate is noted on the visceral pericardium at autopsy (shown in the image). Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this fibrinous exudate?
questions.explanation: Uremic pericarditis results from direct injury to pericardial mesothelial and endothelial cells, causing increased vascular permeability and leakage of fibrinogen-rich plasma onto the serosal surface, which polymerizes into the characteristic shaggy 'bread-and-butter' fibrinous exudate. This is a manifestation of the coagulation system being activated as part of the acute inflammatory response, distinguishing fibrinous pericarditis from a simple serous or hemorrhagic effusion. Chronic passive congestion produces a different picture of venous engorgement without fibrin deposition, and there is no evidence here of antibody-mediated or thrombotic coronary disease.
keypoints: ⭐ Uremic pericarditis is a classic complication of end-stage renal disease, often an indication for urgent dialysis
'Bread-and-butter' pericarditis describes the rough, shaggy gross appearance of fibrinous exudate on opposing pericardial surfaces
Fibrinous pericarditis can also occur post-MI (Dressler syndrome) or with uremia, radiation, or connective tissue disease
questions.imageAlt: Gross photo of heart with shaggy fibrin-rich exudate on the visceral pericardium
questions.imageCaption: Fibrinous ('bread-and-butter') pericarditis in a patient with uremia

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with fever, shaking chills, and shortness of breath. Physical examination shows rales and decreased breath sounds over both lung fields. The patient exhibits grunting respirations, 30 to 35 breaths per minute, with flaring of the nares. The sputum is rusty yellow and displays numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Which of the following mediators of inflammation is chiefly responsible for the development of fever in this patient?
questions.explanation: Exogenous pyrogens released by bacteria stimulate macrophages to secrete endogenous pyrogens, chiefly IL-1 and TNF-α, which act on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center to stimulate local prostaglandin (PGE2) synthesis and reset the body's thermostat upward, producing fever. This is why cyclooxygenase inhibitors such as aspirin, which block PGE2 synthesis, are effective antipyretics. Leukotriene B4 is a potent chemotactic factor rather than a pyrogen, and thromboxane A2/prostacyclin regulate platelet function and vascular tone, not fever.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-1 and TNF-α are the principal endogenous pyrogens; IL-6 also contributes to the acute phase/fever response
Antipyretics work by inhibiting hypothalamic cyclooxygenase and PGE2 synthesis, not by blocking IL-1 directly
Rigors (shaking chills) reflect rapid rises in the hypothalamic set point relative to core temperature

questions.stem: Sputum cultures obtained from the patient described in Question 17 are positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Removal of bacteria from the alveolar air spaces in this patient involves opsonization by complement, an important step in mediating which of the following leukocyte functions?
questions.explanation: Opsonization coats microorganisms with plasma proteins, chiefly IgG and the C3b fragment of complement, that are recognized by specific Fc and complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly enhancing the efficiency of phagocytosis and subsequent intracellular killing. Chemotaxis, margination, and diapedesis describe the sequential steps by which leukocytes travel from the vessel lumen to the tissue, but these processes are driven by chemoattractants and adhesion molecules rather than opsonins. Haptotaxis (directed migration along a substrate-bound gradient) is likewise unrelated to opsonization.
keypoints: ⭐ IgG (via Fc receptors) and C3b (via CR1) are the two most important opsonins in bacterial phagocytosis
Encapsulated organisms like S. pneumoniae resist phagocytosis unless opsonized, explaining susceptibility in asplenic or hypocomplementemic patients
Splenectomized patients are at particular risk for overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms due to loss of opsonin-dependent clearance

questions.stem: Which of the following mediators of inflammation is primarily responsible for secondary injury to alveolar basement membranes and lung parenchyma in the patient described in Questions 17 and 18?
questions.explanation: Neutrophil lysosomal enzymes (proteases such as elastase and collagenase), while essential intracellularly for microbial killing and debridement, can cause substantial collateral tissue injury when released extracellularly during an intense or prolonged inflammatory response, damaging alveolar basement membranes and parenchyma. This double-edged sword nature of neutrophils explains why severe pneumonia can cause structural lung damage beyond what is attributable to the infecting organism itself. The other choices are mediators of inflammation but are less directly implicated in enzymatic tissue destruction.
keypoints: ⭐ Protease/antiprotease balance (e.g., neutrophil elastase vs. α1-antitrypsin) determines the extent of tissue injury in inflammation
Excessive neutrophil enzyme release contributes to ARDS and can worsen outcomes in severe pneumonia
This mechanism parallels the elastase-driven alveolar destruction seen in α1-antitrypsin deficiency emphysema

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of a painful sore on her back. Physical examination reveals a 1-cm abscess over her left shoulder. Biopsy of the lesion shows vasodilation and leukocyte margination (shown in the image). What glycoprotein mediates initial tethering of segmented neutrophils to endothelial cells in this skin lesion?
questions.explanation: Selectins (E-selectin on endothelium, P-selectin on platelets/endothelium, L-selectin on leukocytes) are sugar-binding glycoproteins that mediate the initial, low-affinity tethering and rolling of neutrophils along activated endothelium — the first step of the leukocyte adhesion cascade. Firm adhesion and arrest are subsequently mediated by integrins, which is a distinct, later step. Cadherins mediate cell-cell adhesion within tissues rather than leukocyte-endothelial interactions, and entactin/laminin are basement membrane structural proteins uninvolved in adhesion cascade signaling.
