keypoints: ⭐ Leukocyte adhesion cascade: selectin-mediated rolling → chemokine activation → integrin-mediated firm adhesion → transmigration (diapedesis)
E-selectin is stored in Weibel-Palade bodies and rapidly redistributed to the endothelial luminal surface upon activation
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II results from defective selectin ligand (sialyl-Lewis X) synthesis
questions.imageAlt: Skin biopsy showing vasodilation and leukocyte margination along vessel wall
questions.imageCaption: Leukocyte margination in a cutaneous abscess (carbuncle)

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy receives a laceration on his forehead during an ice hockey game. When he is first attended to by the medic, there is blanching of the skin around the wound. Which of the following mechanisms accounts for this transient reaction to neurogenic and chemical stimuli at the site of injury?
questions.explanation: The initial vascular response to acute injury is a brief, transient constriction of precapillary arterioles, producing the momentary pallor (blanching) seen immediately after trauma. This is quickly followed by arteriolar vasodilation (active hyperemia), which produces the redness and warmth of established acute inflammation. None of the other choices describe a process that causes transient skin blanching; postcapillary venule changes and ischemic necrosis are not features of this immediate neurogenic reflex.
keypoints: ⭐ Sequence: transient arteriolar vasoconstriction (blanching) → vasodilation/active hyperemia (rubor, calor) → increased permeability (tumor)
This initial vasoconstriction is a neurogenic reflex, distinct from the later chemically-mediated vasodilation
Cardinal signs of acute inflammation are rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, and functio laesa

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with asthma presents with respiratory distress. She has a history of allergies and upper respiratory tract infections. She also has history of wheezes associated with exercise. Which of the following mediators of inflammation is the most powerful stimulator of bronchoconstriction and vasoconstriction in this patient?
questions.explanation: Leukotrienes, especially the cysteinyl leukotrienes C4 and D4 (previously called slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis), are generated from arachidonic acid via the lipoxygenase pathway and are the most potent mediators of bronchoconstriction and vasoconstriction in asthma, driving much of the airway obstruction and mucus hypersecretion seen clinically. This is the pharmacologic basis for leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) in asthma management. Bradykinin, complement, IL-1, and TNF-α are all inflammatory mediators but do not match leukotrienes' potency in mediating airway smooth muscle contraction.
keypoints: ⭐ Cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) are ~1000-fold more potent bronchoconstrictors than histamine
Leukotrienes are synthesized via 5-lipoxygenase, a pathway targeted by zileuton
Leukotriene B4 (not cysteinyl leukotrienes) is instead a potent neutrophil chemoattractant

questions.stem: Which of the following preformed substances is released from mast cells and platelets, resulting in increased vascular permeability in the lungs of the patient described in Question 23?
questions.explanation: Histamine is stored preformed within mast cell and basophil granules (and to a lesser extent platelet dense granules) and is released immediately upon IgE-mediated mast cell activation, binding H1 receptors on endothelium to cause cell contraction, gap formation, and increased vascular permeability. Unlike histamine, leukotrienes and thromboxane A2 are synthesized de novo from arachidonic acid only after cell activation rather than being stored preformed. Bradykinin and Hageman factor are plasma-derived mediators, not products released from mast cells or platelets.
keypoints: ⭐ Histamine's effects are mediated via H1 receptors on postcapillary venule endothelium
Massive systemic histamine release can cause anaphylactic shock with hypotension and airway edema
Serotonin is another preformed vasoactive amine, stored in platelet dense granules and released on platelet activation

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman complains of recent onset of chest pain, fever, and productive cough with rust-colored sputum. A chest X-ray reveals an infiltrate in the right middle lobe. Sputum cultures are positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Phagocytic cells in this patient's affected lung tissue generate bactericidal hypochlorous acid using which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation: Myeloperoxidase, contained within neutrophil azurophilic granules, catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide plus a halide (typically chloride) into hypochlorous acid (bleach), one of the most powerful bactericidal oxidants generated by phagocytic cells. NADPH oxidase generates the initial superoxide/H2O2 substrate for this reaction but does not itself produce hypochlorous acid. Catalase instead degrades H2O2 to water and oxygen (a detoxifying, not bactericidal, reaction), and cyclooxygenase and superoxide dismutase are unrelated to hypochlorous acid formation.
keypoints: ⭐ MPO-H2O2-halide system is the most potent antimicrobial system in the neutrophil phagolysosome
Myeloperoxidase deficiency increases susceptibility specifically to Candida infections, despite an intact respiratory burst
Rust-colored sputum is the classic finding of pneumococcal (lobar) pneumonia

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman cuts her hand while dicing vegetables in the kitchen. The wound is cleaned and sutured. Five days later, the site of injury contains an abundance of chronic inflammatory cells that actively secrete interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor-α, interferon-α, numerous arachidonic acid derivatives, and various enzymes. Name these cells.
questions.explanation: Macrophages are the master regulatory cell of chronic inflammation and wound healing, secreting a broad array of cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, interferons), arachidonic acid metabolites, growth factors, and proteolytic enzymes that together orchestrate fibroblast proliferation, angiogenesis, and matrix remodeling. No other single cell type has this breadth of secretory and regulatory function during the transition from acute to chronic/reparative inflammation. B and T lymphocytes and plasma cells participate in chronic inflammation but have far more restricted secretory repertoires and do not directly regulate fibroblast/endothelial proliferation.
keypoints: ⭐ Macrophages derive from circulating monocytes and are the dominant cell of the proliferative/repair phase of wound healing (days 3-7)
Macrophage-derived TGF-β and PDGF are key drivers of fibroblast recruitment and collagen synthesis in granulation tissue
M1 (pro-inflammatory) vs. M2 (reparative) macrophage polarization determines the balance of debridement versus tissue repair

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with prostate cancer and bone metastases presents with shaking chills and fever. The peripheral WBC count is 1,000/μL (normal = 4,000 to 11,000/μL). Which of the following terms best describes this hematologic finding?
questions.explanation: Leukopenia is defined simply as an absolute decrease in circulating white blood cell count below the normal reference range, exactly as demonstrated by this patient's WBC of 1,000/μL. It can occur with bone marrow infiltration by metastatic cancer, chronic debilitating illness, malnutrition, or certain infections. Leukocytosis and neutrophilia describe increased, not decreased, WBC counts, pancytopenia specifically requires decreases in all three cell lines (WBC, RBC, platelets) which is not stated here, and a leukemoid reaction describes markedly elevated WBC counts mimicking leukemia.
keypoints: ⭐ Bone marrow metastases (myelophthisis) from prostate cancer can cause marrow failure and cytopenias, including leukopenia
Leukopenia predisposes to serious, sometimes fatal, bacterial infection due to impaired host defense
Distinguish leukopenia (low WBC) from neutropenia (low neutrophils specifically) — the latter is the more clinically relevant subset in infection risk

questions.stem: A 25-year-old machinist is injured by a metal sliver in his left hand. Over the next few days, the wounded area becomes reddened, tender, swollen, and feels warm to the touch. Redness at the site of injury in this patient is caused primarily by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Vasodilation of precapillary arterioles increases blood flow to the site of injury (active hyperemia), producing the redness (rubor) and warmth (calor) that are cardinal signs of acute inflammation. This vasodilation is mediated by chemical mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins, and nitric oxide released in response to tissue injury. Vasoconstriction produces the opposite effect (pallor), and hemorrhage, hemostasis, and neutrophil margination are separate processes that do not directly account for the erythema and warmth observed.
keypoints: ⭐ Rubor and calor result from increased blood flow (vasodilation); tumor results from increased vascular permeability
Histamine, PGE2, and PGI2 are key vasodilatory mediators of active hyperemia
Active hyperemia (arteriolar dilation) is distinct from passive/congestive hyperemia caused by venous outflow obstruction

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with AIDS is admitted to the hospital with a 3-week history of chest pain and shortness of breath. An X-ray film of the chest shows bilateral nodularities of the lungs. A CT-guided lung biopsy is shown in the image. The multinucleated cell in the center of this field is most likely derived from which of the following inflammatory cells?
questions.explanation: Granulomas are composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells formed by the cytoplasmic fusion of activated macrophages; when nuclei are arranged peripherally in a horseshoe pattern, the cell is termed a Langhans giant cell. This pattern is characteristic of granulomatous disease, common in immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS who develop opportunistic mycobacterial or fungal lung infections. None of the other listed cell types (basophils, endothelial cells, myofibroblasts, smooth muscle cells) form multinucleated giant cells within granulomas.
keypoints: ⭐ Langhans giant cells have peripherally arranged ('horseshoe') nuclei; foreign body giant cells have randomly scattered nuclei
AIDS patients with bilateral pulmonary nodularities should be evaluated for mycobacterial (including atypical), fungal (Histoplasma, Cryptococcus), or Pneumocystis infection
Granuloma formation requires intact cell-mediated (Th1/IFN-γ) immunity, which is why granulomas may be poorly formed in advanced AIDS
questions.imageAlt: Lung biopsy showing a multinucleated giant cell within a granuloma
questions.imageCaption: Multinucleated (Langhans-type) giant cell derived from macrophage fusion

questions.stem: A 59-year-old alcoholic man is brought to the emergency room with a fever (38.7°C/103°F) and foul-smelling breath. A chest X-ray reveals a pulmonary abscess in the right lower lobe. The patient subsequently develops acute bronchopneumonia and dies. Microscopic examination of the lungs at autopsy is shown in the image. Activation of phospholipase A2 in these intra-alveolar cells resulted in the formation of which of the following mediators of inflammation?
questions.explanation: Phospholipase A2 cleaves membrane phospholipids (chiefly phosphatidylcholine) to liberate free arachidonic acid, the substrate for both the cyclooxygenase pathway (prostaglandins, thromboxanes) and the lipoxygenase pathway (leukotrienes). This is the rate-limiting step generating essentially all arachidonic acid-derived inflammatory mediators. cAMP, cGMP, diacylglycerol, and inositol trisphosphate are second messengers generated by different enzymatic pathways (adenylyl cyclase, guanylyl cyclase, and phospholipase C, respectively), not by phospholipase A2.
keypoints: ⭐ Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (via lipocortin/annexin A1 induction), blocking arachidonic acid release upstream of both COX and LOX pathways
Aspiration pneumonia with foul-smelling sputum in an alcoholic patient suggests anaerobic lung abscess (e.g., Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus)
The right lower lobe is a common site for aspiration due to the more vertical orientation of the right mainstem bronchus
questions.imageAlt: Lung histology showing intra-alveolar neutrophils in bronchopneumonia
questions.imageCaption: Acute bronchopneumonia with neutrophil-filled alveolar spaces

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with a 2-week history of puffiness around her eyes and swelling of the legs and ankles. Laboratory studies show hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria. The urinary sediment contains no inflammatory cells or red blood cells. Which of the following terms describes this patient's peripheral edema?
questions.explanation: This child has nephrotic syndrome, with heavy proteinuria causing hypoalbuminemia and a consequent drop in plasma oncotic pressure; the resulting noninflammatory, protein-poor peripheral edema fluid is termed a transudate. An exudate, by contrast, is protein-rich fluid typically associated with inflammation and often containing cells, which is inconsistent with the bland urinary sediment described. Lymphedema results from lymphatic obstruction (e.g., surgery, infection, malignancy), not from hypoalbuminemia, and hydropic change/effusion do not correctly describe this peripheral (interstitial) fluid accumulation.
keypoints: ⭐ Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, typically steroid-responsive
Nephrotic syndrome triad: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, and edema; often with hyperlipidemia
Bland urinary sediment (no RBCs/WBCs/casts) helps distinguish nephrotic from nephritic syndromes

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman develops a sore, red, hot, swollen left knee. She has no history of trauma and no familial history of joint disease. Fluid aspirated from the joint space shows an abundance of segmented neutrophils. Transendothelial migration of acute inflammatory cells into this patient's joint space was mediated primarily by which of the following families of proteins?
questions.explanation: Integrins are cell-surface adhesion molecules activated by chemokines that mediate firm adhesion and subsequent transendothelial migration (diapedesis) of leukocytes into inflamed tissue, following the initial selectin-mediated rolling step. This is the key adhesion family responsible for neutrophils leaving the vasculature to enter the joint space in this presentation of acute (likely gonococcal) septic arthritis. Entactin, fibrillin, fibronectin, and laminin are extracellular matrix structural proteins that maintain tissue architecture and support wound healing, but they are not the primary mediators of leukocyte transmigration.
keypoints: ⭐ β2 integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) bind ICAM-1 on endothelium for firm adhesion prior to transmigration
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I results from defective β2 integrin (CD18) synthesis, causing recurrent bacterial infections with poor pus formation
A young, sexually active patient with acute monoarticular arthritis should be evaluated for disseminated gonococcal infection

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is discovered to have metastatic breast cancer. One week after receiving her first dose of chemotherapy, she develops bacterial pneumonia. Which of the following best explains this patient's susceptibility to bacterial infection?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic chemotherapy suppresses bone marrow production of rapidly dividing cells, and neutrophils — with their short half-life — are especially vulnerable, producing chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, the most common cause of impaired host defense and infection susceptibility in cancer patients undergoing treatment. Chemotherapy does not deplete serum complement levels or specifically impair the neutrophil oxidative (respiratory) burst in surviving cells; the deficit is quantitative (too few neutrophils), not qualitative. Lymphocytosis is the opposite of what would be expected and does not explain increased bacterial susceptibility.
keypoints: ⭐ Febrile neutropenia (ANC <500/μL with fever) is a medical emergency requiring prompt empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics
Neutrophil nadir typically occurs 7-14 days after a chemotherapy cycle, matching this patient's 1-week timeline
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is used prophylactically in high-risk chemotherapy regimens to reduce neutropenia duration

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man develops weakness, malaise, cough with bloody sputum, and night sweats. A chest X-ray reveals numerous apical densities bilaterally. Exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis was documented 20 years ago, and M. tuberculosis is identified in the sputum. The patient subsequently dies of respiratory insufficiency. The lungs are examined at autopsy (shown in the image). Which of the following best characterizes the histopathologic features of this pulmonary lesion?
questions.explanation: The image shows a necrotizing granuloma with a caseous necrotic center surrounded by histiocytes, giant cells, and fibrous tissue — the defining histologic pattern of granulomatous inflammation, classically produced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis as well as fungi, leprosy, schistosomiasis, and certain foreign materials. Caseous ('cheese-like') necrosis is a specific hallmark most associated with TB and is distinct from the coagulative, liquefactive, or fibrinoid necrosis patterns seen in other conditions. Acute suppurative inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis do not match the granulomatous, caseating histology described.
keypoints: ⭐ Caseous necrosis is the histologic hallmark of tuberculosis, combining features of both coagulative and liquefactive necrosis
Reactivation TB classically involves the lung apices, where higher oxygen tension favors mycobacterial growth
Granuloma formation requires Th1-driven cell-mediated immunity (IFN-γ activation of macrophages) via the IL-12/IFN-γ axis
questions.imageAlt: Lung autopsy specimen showing a necrotizing (caseating) granuloma
questions.imageCaption: Caseating granuloma of pulmonary tuberculosis

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man experiences acute chest pain and is rushed to the emergency room. Laboratory studies and ECG demonstrate an acute myocardial infarction; however, coronary artery angiography performed 2 hours later does not show evidence of thrombosis. Intravascular thrombolysis that occurred in this patient was mediated by plasminogen activators that were released by which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Vascular endothelial cells near a thrombus produce tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), which converts plasminogen to plasmin and initiates endogenous fibrinolysis, explaining why an initially occlusive coronary thrombus may have resolved (spontaneous thrombolysis) by the time angiography is performed. This endothelial capacity to both promote and limit thrombosis/inflammation is a key homeostatic function of the vascular lining. None of the other listed cell types produce significant quantities of plasminogen activators.
keypoints: ⭐ tPA-based fibrinolytic drugs (alteplase, reteplase) mimic this natural endothelial fibrinolytic pathway for acute MI/stroke therapy
Endothelial cells also express thrombomodulin and produce prostacyclin/NO, contributing to their anticoagulant, antithrombotic phenotype
Spontaneous coronary thrombolysis explains why some MI patients have open arteries on delayed angiography despite clear infarction

questions.stem: Which of the following mediators of inflammation causes relaxation of vascular smooth muscle cells and vasodilation of arterioles at the site of myocardial infarction in the patient described in Question 39?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (formerly known as endothelium-derived relaxing factor) activates guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle, raising cGMP and producing relaxation and vasodilation of arterioles; it also inhibits platelet aggregation and contributes to macrophage-mediated killing of bacteria and tumor cells. Histamine, leukotrienes, and thromboxane A2 all promote smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction or bronchoconstriction) rather than relaxation, placing them in functional opposition to nitric oxide. Bradykinin causes vasodilation via a different (bradykinin B2 receptor) mechanism but is not the primary mediator described in this vascular relaxation pathway.
keypoints: ⭐ NO signals through soluble guanylyl cyclase → increased cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation (same pathway targeted by nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors)
Endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) is constitutively active, while iNOS in macrophages is induced during infection/inflammation
NO and thromboxane A2/prostacyclin (PGI2) act in physiological opposition to balance vascular tone and platelet activity

questions.stem: A 68-year-old coal miner with a history of smoking and emphysema develops severe air-flow obstruction and expires. Autopsy reveals a "black lung," with coal-dust nodules scattered throughout the parenchyma and a central area of dense fibrosis. The coal dust entrapped within this miner's lung was sequestered primarily by which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis results from inhaled carbon particles being phagocytosed by alveolar and interstitial macrophages, which accumulate as dust-laden cells forming coal-dust macules and, when admixed with fibrogenic silica, denser fibrotic nodules (anthracosilicosis). Macrophages are the principal phagocytic cell of the lung's particulate clearance system, distinguishing them from fibroblasts (which lay down the resultant fibrous stroma but do not phagocytose dust) and from endothelial cells, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, none of which are phagocytic dust-clearing cells.
keypoints: ⭐ Coal macules (nonpalpable) and coal nodules (palpable, fibrotic) both consist of dust-laden macrophages, but nodules involve co-exposure to fibrogenic dusts like silica
Progressive massive fibrosis is a severe complication of coal workers' pneumoconiosis with large confluent fibrotic masses
Pulmonary alveolar macrophages are derived from circulating monocytes and are the first line of particulate/microbial clearance in the lung

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with 5 days of fever (38°C/101°F) and sore throat. She reports that she has felt fatigued for the past week and has difficulty swallowing. A physical examination reveals generalized lymphadenopathy. If this patient has a viral infection, a CBC will most likely show which of the following hematologic findings?
questions.explanation: This presentation (fever, pharyngitis, fatigue, generalized lymphadenopathy) is classic for infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus, and acute viral infections characteristically produce absolute peripheral blood lymphocytosis as antigen-specific and reactive (atypical) lymphocytes expand. Neutrophilia is instead the hallmark of acute bacterial infection, and eosinophilia is characteristic of parasitic or allergic disease, not acute viral illness. Leukopenia and thrombocythemia are not typical features of infectious mononucleosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Infectious mononucleosis shows atypical (reactive) CD8+ T lymphocytes responding to EBV-infected B cells, seen on peripheral smear
Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is the classic rapid diagnostic screen for EBV mononucleosis
Splenomegaly is common in mono and warrants avoiding contact sports due to splenic rupture risk

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of febrile illness and chest pain. She has an erythematous, macular facial rash and tender joints, particularly in her left wrist and elbow. A CBC shows mild anemia and thrombocytopenia. Corticosteroids are prescribed for the patient. This medication induces the synthesis of an inhibitor of which of the following enzymes in inflammatory cells?
questions.explanation: This patient's presentation (facial rash, arthritis, cytopenias, serositis) is consistent with systemic lupus erythematosus. Corticosteroids induce synthesis of lipocortin (annexin A1), which inhibits phospholipase A2 and thereby blocks the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids — the substrate for both the cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways — giving corticosteroids broader anti-inflammatory action than NSAIDs, which only inhibit cyclooxygenase downstream. Myeloperoxidase and superoxide dismutase are unrelated to this mechanism, and phospholipase C/lipoxygenase are not the direct targets of corticosteroid-induced inhibitors.
keypoints: ⭐ Corticosteroids act 'upstream' of NSAIDs by blocking phospholipase A2, shutting down both prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis simultaneously
Chronic corticosteroid use carries risks including adrenal atrophy, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, and increased infection risk
The malar (butterfly) rash, arthritis, and cytopenias in this vignette are classic SLE features (see also Question 46)

questions.stem: The patient described in Question 45 is noted to have increased serum levels of ceruloplasmin, fibrinogen, α2-macroglobulin, serum amyloid A protein, and C-reactive protein. Together, these markers belong to which of the following families of proteins?
questions.explanation: Acute phase proteins are synthesized primarily by the liver in response to cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) released during systemic inflammation, and the group includes CRP, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin, and α2-macroglobulin among others. Elevated acute phase reactants, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate they influence, are used clinically to monitor disease activity in inflammatory conditions such as SLE. None of the other listed categories (anaphylatoxins, platelet activation inhibitors, protease inhibitors specifically, or coagulation regulators) accurately groups this full panel of markers, even though some acute phase proteins (e.g., α2-macroglobulin) also happen to have protease-inhibitory activity.
keypoints: ⭐ IL-6 is the dominant cytokine driving hepatic acute phase protein synthesis, particularly CRP and fibrinogen
CRP is widely used clinically as a marker of systemic inflammation and infection severity
ESR elevation reflects increased fibrinogen promoting red cell rouleaux formation, an indirect marker of the acute phase response

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with acute chest pain and shortness of breath. Cardiac catheterization demonstrates occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Laboratory studies and ECG are consistent with acute myocardial infarction. Which of the following is the most likely pathologic finding in the affected heart muscle 4 weeks later?
questions.explanation: By 4 weeks after a myocardial infarction, the necrotic myocardium has been replaced by mature, collagen-rich scar tissue. Coagulative necrosis appears at about 24 hours, neutrophils and macrophages dominate over the next 2-5 days, and capillary-rich granulation tissue invades toward the end of the first week; scar formation follows over subsequent weeks to months. Granulomatous inflammation does not occur after an ischemic infarct, and vascular congestion/edema reflect acute inflammation rather than a 4-week-old infarct.
keypoints: ⭐ Timeline: coagulative necrosis (~24h) → neutrophils/macrophages (2-5 days) → granulation tissue (end of week 1) → collagen scar (weeks-months)
Myocardium has essentially no regenerative capacity, so healing is by fibrosis rather than regeneration
Mature scar is composed predominantly of type I collagen, which confers tensile strength

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy falls on a rusty nail and punctures his skin. The wound is cleaned and covered with sterile gauze. Which of the following is the initial event in the healing process?
questions.explanation: Wound repair begins with hemorrhage and formation of a fibrin clot (thrombus), which fills the tissue gap, is rich in fibronectin, and dries into a scab that serves as a barrier against microorganisms and fluid loss. Platelets within the clot are an early source of growth factors. Acute inflammatory cell accumulation and macrophage phagocytosis occur after clot formation, myofibroblast differentiation begins around day 3, and collagen/proteoglycan deposition occurs later still.
keypoints: ⭐ Sequence: fibrin clot → acute inflammatory infiltrate → macrophage debridement → myofibroblast/fibroblast proliferation → matrix deposition
The clot is fibronectin-rich and provides a provisional scaffold for migrating cells
Platelets trapped in the clot release growth factors (e.g., PDGF) that initiate the repair cascade

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man dies 4 years after developing congestive heart failure. He had a history of multiple myocardial infarcts over the past 10 years. A trichrome stain of heart muscle at autopsy is shown in the image. What is the predominant type of collagen found in this mature scar tissue?
questions.explanation: A mature scar is composed primarily of type I collagen, which is deposited after the temporary type III collagen-rich matrix of granulation tissue is remodeled; extracellular cross-linking of type I collagen progressively increases wound tensile strength. Type II collagen is found in cartilage, type IV collagen in basement membranes, and types V and VI are found in various other organs, not as the predominant scar collagen.
keypoints: ⭐ Granulation tissue matrix contains type III collagen; mature scar is remodeled to predominantly type I collagen
Trichrome stains highlight collagen (blue/green) against myocardial fibers (red), useful for identifying old infarct scars
Cross-linking of type I collagen fibers is what confers the scar's mechanical strength
questions.imageAlt: Trichrome stain of myocardium showing blue-green collagenous scar replacing necrotic muscle
questions.imageCaption: Trichrome stain of mature myocardial infarct scar (blue-green = collagen)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman sustains a deep, open laceration over her right forearm in a motorcycle accident. The wound is cleaned and sutured. Which of the following cell types mediates contraction of the wound to facilitate healing?
questions.explanation: Myofibroblasts mediate wound contraction (and, when exaggerated, pathologic contracture). They express alpha-smooth muscle actin, desmin, and vimentin, and exert contractile force by forming syncytia joined by tight junctions. Fibroblasts are typically solitary collagen-producing cells rather than contractile, endothelial cells drive angiogenesis, and neither macrophages nor smooth muscle cells mediate wound contraction.
keypoints: ⭐ Myofibroblasts express alpha-smooth muscle actin and respond to vasoactive/smooth-muscle-acting drugs
Excessive myofibroblast contractile activity produces wound contracture, a deforming complication most seen after burns
Myofibroblasts differentiate from fibroblasts/mesenchymal stem cells under the influence of TGF-beta

questions.stem: During the next 3 months, the wound heals with formation of a linear scar. Which of the following nutritional factors is required for proper collagen assembly in the scar tissue of the patient described in Question 4?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a cofactor required for hydroxylation of proline (and lysine) residues during collagen synthesis. Deficiency (scurvy) produces abnormally weak collagen with poor tensile strength, resulting in impaired wound healing and even dehiscence of previously healed wounds. None of the other listed vitamins/nutrients are required for collagen hydroxylation and assembly.
keypoints: ⭐ Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impairs prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase activity, weakening collagen cross-linking
Clinical scurvy features (bleeding gums, poor wound healing, perifollicular hemorrhages) reflect defective collagen
Wound dehiscence can occur in previously well-healed wounds if vitamin C deficiency develops later

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with diabetes develops an ulcer on her right leg (shown in the image). The ulcer bed is covered with granulation tissue. Which of the following are the principal cellular components found in the bed of this wound?
choices: Smooth muscle cells and Merkel cells
questions.explanation: Granulation tissue is composed principally of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (which derive from mesenchymal stem cells and produce matrix) and proliferating capillary endothelial cells (angiogenesis), which together support the metabolic demands of healing. Macrophages are also present as a growth-factor source but are not the defining component. The other cell combinations listed are not the principal constituents of granulation tissue.
keypoints: ⭐ Granulation tissue = fibroblasts/myofibroblasts + proliferating capillaries (angiogenesis)
Macrophages supply growth factors and perform phagocytosis but are a secondary, not principal, component
Once healing is complete, most granulation-tissue capillaries regress, leaving a pale, avascular scar
questions.imageAlt: Diabetic leg ulcer with a beefy-red granulation tissue base
questions.imageCaption: Diabetic lower-extremity ulcer with granulation tissue in the wound bed

questions.stem: Which of the following proteins helps stimulate healing and angiogenesis in the wound of the patient described in Question 6?
questions.explanation: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs, including collagenase, stromelysin, and gelatinase) degrade extracellular matrix proteins, enabling cell migration, and also release bioactive molecules stored in the matrix, promoting healing and angiogenesis. Alpha1-antitrypsin and alpha2-macroglobulin are endogenous inhibitors that limit MMP activity, lysozyme is a neutrophil product that degrades bacterial cell walls, and caspase-9 is an apoptosis mediator, not a healing-promoting protease.
keypoints: ⭐ MMPs degrade matrix proteins and disrupt cell-cell adhesions, facilitating cell migration during repair
MMP activity is regulated by endogenous inhibitors such as alpha1-antitrypsin and alpha2-macroglobulin
MMPs can liberate matrix-bound growth factors, further promoting angiogenesis and healing

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents for repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Severe complicated atherosclerosis is noted at surgery, prompting concern for embolism of atheromatous material to the kidneys and other organs. If the patient were to develop a renal cortical infarct as a result of surgery, which of the following would be the most likely outcome?
questions.explanation: A large renal cortical infarct heals by scar formation (fibrosis) because the underlying extracellular matrix framework is destroyed, precluding complete regeneration. Renal regenerative capacity is greatest in cortical tubules, less in medullary tubules, and absent in glomeruli, but even cortical tubule regeneration cannot fully restore an infarcted region with a destroyed matrix scaffold. Chronic and granulomatous inflammation and hemangioma formation are not expected sequelae of a cortical infarct.
keypoints: ⭐ Regenerative capacity gradient in kidney: cortical tubules > medullary tubules > glomeruli (none)
Destruction of the extracellular matrix scaffold in a large infarct precludes true regeneration, favoring scar
Renal tubule repair after injury may involve proliferation of endogenous renal progenitor (stem) cells

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a painless lesion on her right ear lobe (shown in the image). She reports that her ears were pierced 4 months ago. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this lesion?
choices: Clonal expansion of smooth muscle cells
Increased growth of capillary endothelial cells
Increased turnover of extracellular matrix proteoglycans
questions.explanation: This lesion is a keloid, an exuberant scar that extends beyond the original wound margins and often recurs after excision; it is more common in dark-skinned individuals. Keloids show an altered type III-to-type I collagen ratio and overexpression of fibronectin, suggestive of a 'maturation arrest' in normal scar remodeling. The other choices do not explain keloid pathogenesis.
keypoints: ⭐ Keloids extend beyond the original wound border, unlike hypertrophic scars which stay within it
Higher incidence in dark-skinned individuals; surgical excision alone is often complicated by recurrence
Altered type III:I collagen ratio and fibronectin overexpression support a maturation-arrest mechanism
questions.imageAlt: Firm, raised, hyperpigmented nodular lesion at the ear-piercing site of the earlobe
questions.imageCaption: Keloid arising at an ear-piercing site

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes lumpectomy for breast cancer. One month following surgery, she notices a firm 0.3-cm nodule along one edge of the surgical incision. Biopsy of this nodule reveals chronic inflammatory cells, multinucleated giant cells, and extensive fibrosis. The multinucleated cells in this nodule most likely formed in response to which of the following pathogenic stimuli?
questions.explanation: Granulomatous inflammation, a subtype of chronic inflammation, develops when macrophages cannot digest an injurious agent such as retained suture material or talc; macrophages fuse to form multinucleated giant cells around the foreign material. Bacterial and viral infections and neoplastic cells typically elicit different inflammatory patterns, and lymphatic obstruction does not produce granulomas.
keypoints: ⭐ Foreign-body granulomas classically form around indigestible material such as suture, talc, or splinters
Multinucleated giant cells arise from fusion of macrophages attempting to engulf large or indigestible particles
Consider retained suture material whenever a firm nodule develops at a surgical incision site

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with a history of alcoholism presents with yellow discoloration of his skin and sclerae. Laboratory studies show elevated serum levels of liver enzymes (AST and ALT). A trichrome stain of a liver biopsy is shown in the image. A similar pattern of regeneration and fibrosis would be expected in the liver of a patient with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The image shows cirrhosis, broad collagenous septa (blue on trichrome) surrounding regenerative hepatocyte nodules lacking central veins, obstructing blood and bile flow. Chronic liver injury such as chronic viral hepatitis produces this same pattern of ongoing injury, regeneration, and progressive fibrosis. Acute toxic injury and fulminant necrosis, if the patient survives, tend to regenerate without this fibrotic pattern; hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with tumor-related fibrosis rather than diffuse cirrhotic change, and portal vein thrombosis does not itself cause hepatic fibrosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Cirrhosis = regenerative nodules (lacking central veins) surrounded by fibrous septa, disrupting vascular/biliary architecture
Alcoholic liver disease and chronic viral hepatitis are both classic causes of this cirrhotic pattern
Portal hypertension and jaundice result despite adequate numbers of regenerated but disconnected hepatocytes
questions.imageAlt: Trichrome stain of liver showing regenerative hepatocyte nodules encircled by blue fibrous septa
questions.imageCaption: Trichrome stain of cirrhotic liver with regenerative nodules and fibrous septa

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy trips at school and scrapes the palms of his hands. The wounds are cleaned and covered with sterile gauze. Which of the following terms best characterizes the healing of these superficial abrasions?
questions.explanation: Superficial abrasions that do not extend through the full thickness of the epidermis heal by regeneration, mediated by stem/stable cells that progress through the cell cycle and fully restore normal tissue structure and function via cellular migration and reepithelialization. Fibrosis and granulation tissue formation characterize repair of deeper wounds with tissue loss, and primary/secondary intention describe healing patterns of deeper wounds rather than superficial abrasions.
keypoints: ⭐ Superficial epidermal injury heals by regeneration (full restoration), not fibrosis, because the basement membrane and dermal scaffold are intact
Reepithelialization is driven mainly by cell migration from wound margins, not proliferation alone
Deeper wounds involving dermal loss instead require granulation tissue and scar formation

questions.stem: Which of the following cellular processes helps restore normal epithelial structure and function in the patient described in Question 12?
choices: Collagen and fibronectin-rich extracellular matrix deposition
Contact inhibition of epithelial cell growth and motility
questions.explanation: Reestablishment of an intact, contiguous basal epithelial layer triggers contact inhibition of growth and motility: once epithelial continuity is restored, migration and mitosis cease and normal maturation/shedding resumes. The other choices (matrix deposition, myofibroblast contraction, platelet-driven coagulation, angiogenesis) are features of deeper wound healing, not superficial epidermal regeneration.
keypoints: ⭐ Contact inhibition halts epithelial migration/mitosis once basal cells reestablish cell-cell contact
Loss of contact inhibition (e.g., in neoplasia) allows unchecked epithelial proliferation
Basal cells at the wound margin become activated, migrate, and divide until continuity is restored

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a benign nevus removed from her back under local anesthesia. Which of the following families of cell adhesion molecules is the principal component of the "provisional matrix" that forms during early wound healing?
questions.explanation: Fibronectins are adhesive glycoproteins widely distributed in stromal connective tissue that are deposited at the injury site and cross-linked to fibrin, collagen, and other matrix components by transglutaminases, forming the provisional wound matrix during the first several hours. Fibronectin and associated debris/bacterial products also act as chemoattractants for cells recruited to the wound. Selectins mediate initial leukocyte-endothelial adhesion (not part of the matrix); cadherins and integrins are cell-surface adhesion molecules, not matrix components; laminins are basement-membrane glycoproteins.
keypoints: ⭐ Fibronectin forms the cross-linked provisional wound matrix, stabilized to fibrin/collagen by transglutaminases
Fibronectin fragments act as chemoattractants recruiting inflammatory and repair cells to the wound
Contrast with selectins/cadherins/integrins, which are cell-surface adhesion receptors, not matrix proteins

questions.stem: Which of the following families of glycoproteins plays the most important role in regulating the migration and differentiation of leukocytes and connective tissue cells during wound healing in the patient described in Question 14?
questions.explanation: Integrins are transmembrane adhesion receptors at the leading edge of a migrating cell that bind extracellular matrix components, transmitting mechanical and chemical signals that regulate cell survival, proliferation, differentiation, and migration of both leukocytes and connective tissue cells. Cadherins mediate cell-cell adhesion, fibrillins are structural molecules associated with elastic fibers, laminins are basement-membrane glycoproteins, and selectins mediate the initial rolling adhesion of neutrophils in acute inflammation, not directed migration.
keypoints: ⭐ Integrins link the cytoskeleton (via lamellipodia/filopodia) to the extracellular matrix, driving directed cell migration
Fibroblasts extend filopodia; faster, ameboid-moving cells use lamellipodia
Selectins govern the earliest leukocyte-endothelial rolling/adhesion step, distinct from integrin-mediated locomotion

questions.stem: A 29-year-old carpenter receives a traumatic laceration to her left arm. Which of the following is the most important factor that determines whether this wound will heal by primary or secondary intention?
questions.explanation: Healing by primary intention occurs when wound edges are closely apposed with minimal tissue loss, requiring only minimal cell proliferation and neovascularization and producing a small scar. Secondary intention occurs when wound edges are far apart with substantial tissue loss, requiring wound contraction, extensive proliferation, and granulation tissue formation before eventual resorption into a larger, less satisfactory scar. Depth, metabolic status, skin site, and vascular supply all influence overall healing outcome but do not themselves distinguish primary from secondary intention.
keypoints: ⭐ Primary intention = closely apposed edges, minimal tissue loss, small scar; secondary intention = wide gap, substantial tissue loss, granulation tissue and larger scar
Secondary-intention wounds require wound contraction (myofibroblast activity) that primary-intention wounds largely do not
Suturing a laceration converts what might heal by secondary intention into healing by primary intention

questions.stem: Activated fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and capillary sprouts are most abundant in the wound of the patient described in Question 16 at which of the following times after injury?
questions.explanation: Activated fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and capillary sprouts (i.e., granulation tissue) are most abundant 3 to 5 days after injury, as fibroblasts change shape from oval to bipolar and begin synthesizing extracellular matrix proteins. Neutrophils predominate earlier, at 12 to 24 hours, while a mature scar is generally visible by about 2 weeks after injury.
keypoints: ⭐ Wound-healing timeline landmark: granulation tissue (fibroblasts/myofibroblasts/capillaries) peaks at day 3-5
Neutrophil influx precedes this at 12-24 hours; macrophages follow shortly after neutrophils
By about 2 weeks, a primary-intention wound typically shows a mature, well-formed scar

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy receives a deep laceration over his right eyebrow playing ice hockey. The wound is cleaned and sutured. Which of the following describes the principal function of macrophages that are present in the wound 24 to 48 hours after injury?
questions.explanation: Macrophages arrive shortly after neutrophils and persist in the wound for days, with their principal role being phagocytic removal of debris and orchestration of granulation tissue formation via cytokine and chemoattractant release. Antibody production is a function of plasma cells, collagen deposition is performed by fibroblasts, histamine release is characteristic of mast cells/basophils, and wound contraction is mediated by myofibroblasts, not macrophages.
keypoints: ⭐ Macrophages both phagocytose debris and orchestrate subsequent repair via cytokine/growth factor release
Distinguish macrophage function from fibroblast (collagen), myofibroblast (contraction), and plasma cell (antibody) roles
Macrophages persist in the wound longer than the initial neutrophil wave

questions.stem: Which of the following collagens is deposited first during wound healing in the patient described in Question 18?
questions.explanation: Concurrent with fibrinolysis, a temporary matrix of proteoglycans, glycoproteins, and type III collagen is deposited first; this precedes and is later replaced by type I collagen, which imparts greater tensile strength as it becomes cross-linked. Type II collagen is found in cartilage and type IV collagen in basement membranes, neither of which are involved in this early wound matrix; type V collagen is not the initial wound-healing collagen.
keypoints: ⭐ Early wound matrix: type III collagen; mature scar: type I collagen (remodeling over weeks)
TGF-beta enhances collagen/fibronectin synthesis while decreasing MMP-mediated matrix degradation
Extracellular cross-linking of the eventual type I collagen network progressively increases wound strength

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy suffers a concussion during an ice hockey game and is rushed to the emergency room. A CT scan of the brain reveals a cerebral contusion of the left frontal lobe. The boy lies comatose for 3 days but eventually regains consciousness. Which of the following cells is the principal mediator of scar formation in the central nervous system of this patient?
questions.explanation: Central nervous system injury triggers proliferation of astrocytes and microglia (gliosis), which is the CNS equivalent of scar formation and, once established, is permanent. Fibroblasts are the mediators of scarring in most peripheral tissues but not the CNS; neurons and oligodendrocytes do not proliferate significantly in response to injury; and Schwann cells mediate peripheral, not central, nerve repair.
keypoints: ⭐ Gliosis (astrocyte/microglial proliferation) is the CNS analog of fibrous scarring and is permanent once established
Axonal regeneration in the spinal cord can occur up to ~2 weeks post-injury, before gliosis blocks further regrowth
In the CNS, meaningful axonal regeneration occurs almost exclusively in the hypothalamohypophysial region

questions.stem: A 30-year-old firefighter suffers extensive third-degree burns over his arms and hands. This patient is at high risk for developing which of the following complications of wound healing?
questions.explanation: Extensive deep burns heal with substantial myofibroblast-mediated wound contraction; when exaggerated, this produces contracture, a severe deforming complication that can compromise joint movement, particularly conspicuous after serious burns. Dehiscence and incisional hernia relate to surgical wound breakdown, keloid is an exuberant scar (more related to skin type/genetics than burn extent per se), and traumatic neuroma follows nerve transection, not burns.
keypoints: ⭐ Extensive burns over joints are a classic setup for disabling contracture requiring physical therapy/surgical release
Contracture is an exaggeration of normal myofibroblast-driven wound contraction
Contrast contracture (excess contraction) with dehiscence (wound breakdown), a distinct complication

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man suffers a crush injury of his foot, which becomes secondarily infected. He undergoes a below-the-knee amputation. Six months later, the patient complains of chronic pain at the site of amputation. A firm nodule is identified at the scar site. A biopsy of the nodule demonstrates haphazard growth of nerves (shown in the image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Peripheral nerves can regenerate their axons after transection, but if the cut ends are misaligned or prevented from reestablishing continuity by scar/inflammation, a traumatic neuroma forms—a bulbous lesion of disorganized regenerating axons, proliferating Schwann cells, and fibroblasts surrounded by dense collagenous tissue. Ganglioma, ganglioneuroma, and hamartoma are benign neoplasms rather than a reactive/regenerative process, and 'neural nevus' is not the correct terminology for this entity.
keypoints: ⭐ Traumatic neuroma = disorganized regenerating axons + Schwann cells + fibroblasts encased in dense collagen at a transected nerve stump
Classic setting: post-amputation stump pain with a palpable nodule
Unlike a true neoplasm, a neuroma is a reactive/regenerative response to failed nerve continuity
questions.imageAlt: Trichrome-stained biopsy showing a nerve entering a neuroma surrounded by dense blue collagenous tissue
questions.imageCaption: Traumatic neuroma: disorganized nerve fascicles within dense collagenous scar

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of a painful sore on his hand. Physical examination reveals a 0.5-cm abscess on the extensor surface of the left hand that drains a thick, purulent material. Diapedesis of leukocytes into and around this patient's infected wound occurs primarily at which of the following anatomic locations?
questions.explanation: Diapedesis of leukocytes (and plasma leakage) occurs primarily at the level of the postcapillary venule, where endothelial cell activation, loss of vascular integrity, and selectin-mediated leukocyte adhesion initiate emigration of leukocytes and fluid into the extravascular tissue. Leukocytes do not typically undergo diapedesis at lymphatic capillaries, precapillary arterioles, or small dermal arteries/veins.
keypoints: ⭐ Postcapillary venules are the principal site of leukocyte adhesion and diapedesis in acute inflammation
Selectins mediate the initial rolling/adhesion of leukocytes to venular endothelium before transmigration
This anatomic focus explains why perivenular edema and cuffing are common histologic findings in acute inflammation

questions.stem: During the physical examination of a 22-year-old man, a purified protein derivative isolated from Mycobacterium tuberculosis is injected into the skin. Three days later, the injection site appears raised and indurated. Which of the following glycoproteins was directly involved in antigen presentation during the initiation phase of delayed hypersensitivity in this patient?
questions.explanation: The PPD/tuberculin skin test is a classic example of delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity, which peaks 24-48 hours after antigen exposure. In the initiation phase, protein antigens are processed by antigen-presenting cells and displayed on the cell surface bound to class II HLA molecules, which are recognized by CD4+ helper T cells. CD4 (choice A) is the coreceptor on the responding T cell, not the presenting glycoprotein itself, and CD8 (choice B) marks cytotoxic/suppressor T cells that are not the primary responders here. Class I HLA molecules (choice C) present antigen to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells for cell-mediated cytotoxicity, a different pathway. GlyCAM-1 (choice E) is a cell adhesion molecule involved in lymphocyte trafficking, unrelated to antigen presentation.
keypoints: ⭐ Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity peaks at 24-48 hours and is mediated by CD4+ T cells and macrophages, not antibodies
⭐ Class II HLA molecules restrict antigen presentation to CD4+ T helper cells; class I HLA restricts presentation to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
The PPD (tuberculin) test is the prototypical clinical test for prior mycobacterial exposure and intact cell-mediated immunity
Activated CD4+ T cells release cytokines that recruit and activate macrophages, fibroblasts, and other inflammatory cells at the site

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman is involved in an automobile accident and requires a blood transfusion. Five hours later, she becomes febrile and has severe back pain. Laboratory studies show evidence of intravascular hemolysis. It is discovered that type A Rh+ blood was given by mistake to this type B Rh+ patient. Which of the following best explains the development of intravascular hemolysis in this patient?
questions.explanation: An ABO-incompatible transfusion is a type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by preformed antibodies directed against fixed antigens on the transfused erythrocytes. In this case, the patient's preexisting anti-A antibodies bind to A antigens on the transfused red cells, and at sufficient antibody density this fixes complement, generating a membrane attack complex that lyses the cells intravascularly. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (choice A) involves cytolytic leukocytes attacking antibody-coated targets rather than complement-mediated lysis. Delayed-type hypersensitivity (choice C) is T-cell mediated and takes 24-48 hours, immune complex disease (choice D) is a type III reaction, and immediate hypersensitivity (choice E) is IgE-mediated (type I) — none fit this acute intravascular hemolytic picture.
keypoints: ⭐ Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions from ABO mismatch are the prototypical type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction
⭐ Complement fixation by IgM anti-A/anti-B antibodies causes intravascular hemolysis, presenting with fever, flank/back pain, and hemoglobinuria
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia shares the same complement-mediated lytic mechanism against self red cell antigens
Rh incompatibility (unlike ABO) typically causes extravascular hemolysis via IgG and is a concern mainly in repeated exposures (e.g., pregnancy)

questions.stem: What glycoprotein on virally infected hepatocytes provides a target for cell-mediated cytotoxicity in a patient with chronic hepatitis B (jaundice, hepatomegaly, elevated bilirubin, positive HBsAg, HBeAg, and IgG anti-HBcAg)?
questions.explanation: Class I HLA molecules present endogenously synthesized viral peptides (such as those from hepatitis B) on the surface of infected hepatocytes, and this complex is recognized by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes, which then kill the infected cell. This cell-mediated cytotoxicity — not the virus itself — is largely responsible for hepatocyte injury in chronic hepatitis B. CD4 and CD8 (choices A and B) are T-cell coreceptors, not the presenting molecule on the target cell. Class II HLA molecules (choice D) present exogenous antigens to CD4+ helper T cells, a pathway relevant to humoral immunity rather than direct cytotoxic killing of infected cells. GlyCAM-1 (choice E) mediates lymphocyte trafficking via high endothelial venules and is unrelated to antigen presentation.
keypoints: ⭐ Class I HLA molecules are expressed on nearly all nucleated cells and present endogenous (e.g., viral) antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
⭐ Liver injury in chronic hepatitis B is largely immune-mediated (CD8+ T-cell killing of infected hepatocytes) rather than direct viral cytopathic effect
Class II HLA molecules are restricted mainly to professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) and present to CD4+ T cells
HBeAg and HBsAg positivity with IgG anti-HBc indicates ongoing chronic infection, not resolved disease

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman complains of impaired speech and frequent aspiration of food. Physical examination reveals diplopia and drooping eyelids. A mediastinal mass is removed and diagnosed as thymoma. The symptoms of muscle weakness in this patient are caused by antibodies directed against which of the following cellular components?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is a type II hypersensitivity disorder in which autoantibodies bind to and downregulate the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, impairing transmission and causing fatigable muscle weakness that classically affects ocular and bulbar muscles first. It is strongly associated with thymic abnormalities, including thymoma or thymic hyperplasia. Antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels (choice B) instead cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, often paraneoplastic to small cell lung cancer. Desmoglein-3 antibodies (choice C) cause pemphigus vulgaris, and TSH receptor antibodies (choice E) cause Graves disease — neither produces this clinical picture.
keypoints: ⭐ Myasthenia gravis: anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause fatigable weakness worsening with activity, improving with rest
⭐ Thymoma is present in about 10-15% of myasthenia gravis patients; thymic hyperplasia is even more common
Contrast with Lambert-Eaton syndrome: presynaptic anti-calcium channel antibodies, weakness improves with repeated activity, paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer)
Diagnosis supported by edrophonium (Tensilon) test and repetitive nerve stimulation showing decremental response

questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes converts the HIV genome into double-stranded DNA in host cells in a patient with AIDS?
questions.explanation: HIV-1 is an enveloped RNA retrovirus. After the virus enters the cytoplasm of a CD4+ T lymphocyte and is uncoated, its single-stranded RNA genome is copied into double-stranded DNA by the virally encoded enzyme reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase). This proviral DNA is then transported into the nucleus and integrated into the host genome by a separate viral enzyme, integrase (choice C), producing the latent provirus. DNA polymerases Pol-1 and Pol-2 (choices A and B) and topoisomerase (choice E) are host/bacterial replication enzymes not responsible for reverse transcription of the retroviral genome.
keypoints: ⭐ Reverse transcriptase converts HIV genomic RNA into double-stranded proviral DNA — the target of NRTI/NNRTI antiretroviral drugs
⭐ Integrase then inserts the proviral DNA into the host genome — the target of integrase strand-transfer inhibitors (e.g., raltegravir)
The proviral form allows HIV to persist latently, replicating along with host chromosomes for the life of the infected cell
Protease (a third key HIV enzyme, not listed here) cleaves viral polyproteins during virion maturation and is targeted by protease inhibitors

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with a history of asthma and allergies undergoes skin testing to identify potential allergens in her environment. A positive skin reaction to ragweed in this patient would be mediated by which of the following classes of immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation: Allergen skin testing detects immediate (type I) hypersensitivity, which is mediated by IgE bound to high-affinity Fc-epsilon receptors on mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure to allergen, antigen cross-links receptor-bound IgE, triggering mast cell degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators within minutes, producing the wheal-and-flare reaction seen on skin testing. IgG (choice D) mediates type II and III hypersensitivity reactions rather than immediate mast cell degranulation. IgA (choice A) is the principal mucosal immunoglobulin, IgD (choice B) functions mainly as a B-cell receptor, and IgM (choice E) is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response — none trigger immediate hypersensitivity reactions.
keypoints: ⭐ IgE is the cytophilic antibody that sensitizes mast cells/basophils via high-affinity Fc-epsilon receptors, mediating type I hypersensitivity
⭐ Immediate hypersensitivity reactions occur within minutes of allergen exposure in a previously sensitized individual
Severe generalized type I reactions cause bronchoconstriction, airway edema, and circulatory collapse (anaphylaxis)
Skin (wheal-and-flare) testing is the clinical correlate of localized IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation

questions.stem: A neonate develops spastic contractions on the second postpartum day. Laboratory studies show hypocalcemia. MRI studies demonstrate aplasia of the thymus and parathyroid glands. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome results from a developmental defect of the third and fourth pharyngeal (branchial) pouches, causing aplasia or hypoplasia of the thymus and parathyroid glands. Parathyroid aplasia leads to hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcemia, which manifests as neonatal tetany/spastic contractions, while thymic aplasia causes a profound T-cell immunodeficiency. Adenosine deaminase deficiency (choice A) causes severe combined immunodeficiency but not this pattern of parathyroid/thymic aplasia, and common variable immunodeficiency and transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy (choices B and D) are humoral, not developmental, disorders that typically present later in life. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (choice E) presents with eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections, not hypocalcemia.
keypoints: ⭐ DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion affecting third/fourth pharyngeal pouch development
⭐ Classic triad: congenital heart defects (conotruncal anomalies), hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcemia, and thymic aplasia with T-cell deficiency
Neonatal tetany from hypocalcemia is often the presenting feature, since parathyroid aplasia causes early hormone deficiency
Absent thymic shadow on chest imaging is a classic finding supporting the diagnosis

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with a 5-day history of sore throat. His temperature is 38.7°C (103°F). Physical examination reveals inflamed tonsils and swollen cervical lymph nodes. Trafficking and recirculation of blood-borne lymphocytes through the cervical lymph nodes in this patient occurs primarily at which of the following locations?
questions.explanation: Blood-borne B and T lymphocytes enter lymph nodes primarily through specialized postcapillary venules called high endothelial venules (HEVs), whose cuboidal endothelial cells express adhesion molecules that allow lymphocyte binding and diapedesis into the node. Afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels (choices A and B) carry lymph fluid and lymphocytes that have already trafficked through tissue or the node, not blood-borne cells entering directly from the vasculature. Hassall corpuscles (choice C) are structures found in the thymic medulla, unrelated to lymph node trafficking, and Peyer patches (choice E) are organized lymphoid tissue specific to the small intestine.
keypoints: ⭐ High endothelial venules (HEVs) are the primary site of lymphocyte entry from blood into lymph nodes, mediated by specific adhesion molecules (e.g., GlyCAM-1, CD31)
⭐ The cuboidal shape of HEV endothelium reduces flow-mediated shear, facilitating lymphocyte adhesion and transmigration
Lymphocytes exit lymph nodes via efferent lymphatics to re-enter the bloodstream via the thoracic duct, completing the recirculation cycle
Reactive lymphadenopathy (as in this patient's streptococcal pharyngitis) reflects increased lymphocyte trafficking and proliferation within the node

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents for a preschool physical examination. The child has a small head circumference, thin upper lip, and low-bridge nose. She shows evidence of mild mental retardation. Her parents state that she is often "emotional." Which of the following maternal causes of birth defects most likely accounts for these clinicopathologic findings?
questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome results from maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy and produces a triad of growth retardation, CNS dysfunction, and characteristic facial dysmorphology (small head circumference, thin upper lip, low nasal bridge). Affected children frequently show short memory span, impulsiveness, and emotional instability even when IQ is normal. Maternal smoking and poor nutrition can impair fetal growth but do not produce this specific pattern of facial dysmorphology and emotional lability. Congenital syphilis causes protean, non-specific manifestations, and gestational diabetes does not cause mental retardation.
keypoints: ⭐ Fetal alcohol syndrome is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the developed world.
About 20% of affected children have IQ <70 and another 40% have IQ 70-85.
No amount of alcohol has been proven safe at any point in pregnancy.
Alcohol is directly toxic to migrating neurons and can cause holoprosencephaly in severe cases.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old boy is brought to the emergency room for examination of his right arm following a tumble at home. Radiologic examination of the limb reveals a recent fracture of the right ulna and evidence of additional healing fractures. The child is noted to have blue sclerae. This patient most likely carries a mutation in a gene that encodes which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is a group of inherited disorders caused by heterogeneous mutations that all impair synthesis of type I collagen. Type I OI presents with normal appearance at birth but recurrent fractures during infancy and early childhood, described as children being 'fragile as a China doll.' Blue sclerae result from decreased collagen content, which allows the underlying choroidal veins to show through the thinned, translucent sclera. Fibrillin mutations cause Marfan syndrome, and keratin mutations cause epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, neither of which explains this presentation.
keypoints: ⭐ Multiple healing fractures plus blue sclerae in an infant should always prompt consideration of OI before assuming non-accidental trauma (child abuse).
Hearing loss is common in OI due to fusion/fracture of the tiny bones of the middle ear.
OI is genetically heterogeneous (types I-IV) but all forms share a defect in type I collagen.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman gives birth to a stillborn with a severe neural tube defect (neonate shown in the image). This birth defect was caused by an error of morphogenesis that occurred at which of the following stages of development after fertilization?
questions.explanation: Anencephaly is a dysraphic anomaly resulting from failure of the neural tube to close, an injury that occurs between roughly day 23 and day 26 of gestation (within the 20- to 40-day window) when the neural plate normally fuses into the neural tube. Failure of closure prevents formation of the overlying calvarium, skin, and subcutaneous tissue, leaving the exposed brain incompletely formed or absent. Blastocyst formation and implantation occur during days 1-10, which is too early for this defect to arise.
keypoints: ⭐ Neural tube closure is complete by about day 28; this is the critical window for periconceptional folic acid supplementation to be effective.
Anencephaly is the most severe dysraphic anomaly and is incompatible with life.
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and ultrasound are used to screen for open neural tube defects.
questions.imageAlt: Stillborn neonate with anencephaly showing absent calvarium and exposed, malformed brain tissue
questions.imageCaption: Anencephalic stillborn neonate, illustrating a severe neural tube defect from failure of neural tube closure.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is examined by a new family physician who discovers numerous pigmented patches and pedunculated skin tumors on his chest. Biopsy of a tumor discloses a benign neoplasm derived from Schwann cells. Neither the patient's father nor mother shows signs of this disease. This patient most likely carries a mutation in a gene that encodes which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) presents with disfiguring neurofibromas, café-au-lait skin macules, and Lisch nodules of the iris, and is one of the more common autosomal dominant disorders (with about half of cases arising as new sporadic mutations, explaining unaffected parents). The NF1 gene product, neurofibromin, belongs to the family of GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) that normally inactivate ras protein, making NF1 a classic tumor suppressor gene. Loss of GAP activity after a second-hit mutation permits unchecked ras p21 activation, driving neurofibroma formation; ras itself (choice E) is the downstream target being dysregulated, not the mutated gene product.
keypoints: ⭐ NF1 is a tumor suppressor gene whose loss of function unleashes constitutive Ras signaling, distinguishing it mechanistically from oncogene-driven cancers.
Café-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) are classic diagnostic clues alongside neurofibromas.
NF1 should be distinguished from NF2, which involves bilateral acoustic (vestibular schwannomas) and is due to merlin/schwannomin mutations.

questions.stem: The patient described in Question 4 is at increased risk of developing which of the following malignant neoplasms?
questions.explanation: Neurofibrosarcoma (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor) arises within a preexisting neurofibroma in 3-5% of patients with NF1, representing the disease's major malignant complication. NF1 also carries an increased incidence of other neurogenic tumors, including meningioma, optic glioma, and pheochromocytoma. Ganglioneuroma is typically benign, and glioblastoma, serous cystadenocarcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma are not part of the NF1 tumor spectrum.
keypoints: ⭐ Malignant transformation should be suspected in an NF1 patient when a neurofibroma suddenly enlarges or becomes painful.
Optic nerve glioma is a characteristic (often pediatric) NF1-associated CNS tumor.
Pheochromocytoma occurs at increased frequency in NF1 and should be screened for if hypertension develops.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman, at 16 weeks of gestation, visits her obstetrician. A screening test suggests the possibility of a neural tube defect in her fetus. An ultrasound examination shows a 3-cm neural tube defect in the thoracic spine. The screening test that was administered to the mother measured serum levels of which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), combined with ultrasonography, allows detection of virtually all anencephalic fetuses and most open spina bifida defects because AFP leaks from exposed fetal neural tissue and amniotic fluid into the maternal circulation. Levels of albumin, bilirubin, chromogranin, and hCG are not significantly altered by a neural tube defect and are not part of this screening paradigm. AFP is a component of the standard second-trimester quad screen along with hCG, estriol, and inhibin A.
keypoints: ⭐ Elevated maternal serum AFP suggests an open neural tube defect or ventral wall defect (e.g., gastroschisis), whereas low AFP is associated with trisomy 21.
Amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase can confirm an equivocal maternal serum screen.
AFP is the fetal counterpart of albumin, normally produced by the fetal yolk sac and liver.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is found to have extremely pliable skin. His parents note that he bruises easily. His joints can be hyperextended. Biochemical studies demonstrate a deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase. Ultrastructural examination of a skin biopsy of this patient would most likely reveal abnormalities associated with which of the following cell/tissue components?
questions.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are a group of inherited connective tissue disorders featuring skin hyperelasticity, fragility, joint hypermobility, and a bleeding diathesis, all stemming from a generalized defect in collagen structure, synthesis, secretion, or degradation (here caused by lysyl hydroxylase deficiency, which impairs collagen cross-linking). Because sutures do not hold well in this fragile tissue, surgical wound dehiscence is common. None of the other cytoskeletal or membrane components listed (actin-myosin, glycocalyx, intermediate filaments, mitochondria) are primarily affected in EDS.
keypoints: ⭐ Lysyl hydroxylase deficiency defines EDS type VI (kyphoscoliotic type); other EDS subtypes involve different collagen-processing enzymes or collagen genes themselves.
Joint hypermobility in EDS predisposes to recurrent dislocations.
Vascular type EDS (type IV, COL3A1 mutation) carries the highest risk of spontaneous arterial or bowel rupture.

questions.stem: A neonate is born with severe motor dysfunction involving the lower extremities. Radiologic studies show that vertebral bodies in the lumbar region lack posterior arches. The vertebral defects are covered by a thin membrane. The space underneath the membrane contains a mass of tissue that is composed of meninges and spinal cord. The parents ask for information regarding risks for similar birth defects in their future offspring. You mention that dietary supplementation of the maternal diet has been shown to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects. What is this substance?
questions.explanation: This neonate has a meningomyelocele, a dysraphic neural tube defect of polygenic origin like spina bifida and anencephaly. Periconceptional folic acid supplementation has been shown to lower the incidence of neural tube defects, prompting the FDA in 1998 to require folic acid fortification of enriched grain products. Thiamine deficiency causes beri-beri (polyneuropathy, edema, heart failure), and vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia; neither is linked to neural tube defect prevention, and niacin and B6 are likewise unrelated.
keypoints: ⭐ Women planning pregnancy are advised to take 0.4 mg folic acid daily, increased to 4 mg if there is a prior neural tube defect pregnancy.
Folic acid must be started before conception since the neural tube closes by about day 28, often before pregnancy is recognized.
Antiepileptic drugs (e.g., valproate) that impair folate metabolism increase neural tube defect risk.

questions.stem: The parents of an infant with cleft lip and palate (infant shown in the image) visit a genetic counselor to discuss the chance that a similar birth defect will occur in their future offspring. In addition to teratogen exposure and multifactorial inheritance, which of the following is an important cause of this error of morphogenesis?
choices: First pregnancy before 25 years of age
questions.explanation: Cleft lip and palate arise from disturbed fusion of the frontal prominence with the maxillary process around day 35 of gestation and classically exemplify multifactorial inheritance, in which multiple genes interact with environmental teratogens (e.g., rubella, anticonvulsants). Beyond multifactorial inheritance and teratogens, cleft lip/palate is also commonly seen as a feature of malformation syndromes caused by structural chromosomal abnormalities. Maternal age, Rh incompatibility, and Turner syndrome are not established causes of cleft lip/palate.
keypoints: ⭐ Recurrence risk rises sharply with family history: about 4% after one affected child, increasing to 9% after two affected children.
Incidence of cleft lip (with or without cleft palate) is about 1 in 1,000 births; isolated cleft palate is about 1 in 2,500.
Sons of women with cleft lip have a fourfold higher risk of the defect than sons of affected fathers, reflecting complex multifactorial transmission.
questions.imageAlt: Infant with a unilateral cleft lip and cleft palate exposing the nasal cavity and upper dental arch
questions.imageCaption: Neonate with cleft lip and palate, a multifactorial error of morphogenesis in fusion of the frontal prominence and maxillary process.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he tires easily. Physical examination reveals weakness in the pelvic and shoulder girdles and enlargement of the child's calf muscle. Serum levels of creatine kinase are elevated. A biopsy of calf muscle shows marked variation in size and shape of muscle fibers. There are foci of muscle fiber necrosis, with myophagocytosis, regenerating fibers, and fibrosis. Molecular diagnostic assays would most likely show alterations in the length of the primary transcript for which of the following muscle-associated proteins?
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked disease of progressive muscle degeneration, particularly of the pelvic and shoulder girdles, caused by deficiency of dystrophin, a membrane cytoskeletal protein linked via the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex to extracellular laminin. The dystrophin gene is enormous, and large deletions/duplications alter the length of its primary transcript, which is the basis for molecular diagnosis; loss of dystrophin destabilizes the sarcolemma, predisposing myocytes to contraction-induced injury and elevated creatine kinase. Glycogen phosphorylase mutations cause McArdle disease, not DMD, and the other cytoskeletal proteins listed are not the primary defect.
keypoints: ⭐ Calf pseudohypertrophy in DMD results from fatty and fibrous tissue replacing degenerated muscle, not true muscle hypertrophy.
Becker muscular dystrophy is a milder allelic variant caused by partially functional (rather than absent) dystrophin.
