DMD is X-linked recessive, so it almost exclusively affects boys; female carriers are usually asymptomatic.

questions.stem: What will be the likely cause of death in the patient described in Question 21?
questions.explanation: As Duchenne muscular dystrophy progresses, dystrophin deficiency affects cardiac as well as skeletal muscle, and cardiac symptoms become almost universal in advanced disease, with cardiomyopathy a common cause of death (mean age at death around 17 years). More than half of boys with DMD fail to walk by 18 months, and over 90% are wheelchair-bound by age 11, but it is cardiac rather than renal, cerebrovascular, or embolic disease that most often proves fatal. Respiratory insufficiency can also contribute late in the disease but cardiomyopathy is the classic cause emphasized for DMD.
keypoints: ⭐ Because dystrophin is expressed in cardiac muscle, all DMD patients should be screened periodically with echocardiography for dilated cardiomyopathy.
Death in DMD typically occurs in the late teens to twenties.
Respiratory muscle weakness also contributes to morbidity (recurrent pneumonia, hypoventilation) but cardiomyopathy is the emphasized cause of death here.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man complains about his inability to conceive a child. On physical examination, the patient is noted to be tall (6 ft, 5 in) and exhibits gynecomastia and testicular atrophy. Laboratory studies demonstrate increased serum levels of follicle-stimulating hormone. Cytogenetic studies reveal a chromosomal abnormality. What is the most common cause of this patient's chromosomal abnormality?
questions.explanation: This presentation of tall stature, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, and elevated FSH describes Klinefelter syndrome (testicular dysgenesis), most commonly resulting from an extra X chromosome (47,XXY karyotype) in about 80% of cases. This additional X chromosome most often arises from nondisjunction during gametogenesis (meiosis), with paternal meiosis I nondisjunction responsible for about half of cases, producing an XY sperm that fertilizes a normal oocyte. Isochromosome formation, nonreciprocal translocation, ring chromosome formation, and trinucleotide repeat expansion are mechanisms seen in other genetic diseases, not the typical cause of Klinefelter syndrome.
keypoints: ⭐ Klinefelter syndrome occurs in about 1 in 1,000 male births, an incidence comparable to Down syndrome.
Elevated FSH/LH with low testosterone reflects primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism from seminiferous tubule dysgenesis.
Klinefelter patients have increased risk of extragonadal germ cell tumors and breast cancer relative to other men.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl complains that she has not started menstruating like other girls her age. The patient is short (4 ft, 11 in) and has a thick-webbed neck. Physical examination reveals widely spaced nipples and poor breast development. If this patient's genetic disease was caused by nondisjunction during mitosis of a somatic cell in the early stages of embryogenesis, which of the following is the patient's most likely karyotype?
questions.explanation: This patient has Turner syndrome, characterized by short stature, webbed neck, and primary amenorrhea due to complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome. When mitotic (rather than meiotic) nondisjunction occurs in early embryogenesis, mosaicism results, in which two or more karyotypically distinct cell lines coexist; the 45,X/46,XX mosaic karyotype accounts for about 15% of Turner syndrome cases and tends to produce a milder phenotype. Pure 45,X monosomy (choice A) arises from meiotic, not mitotic, nondisjunction; 45,X/46,XY mosaicism occurs in about 5% of cases; 47,XX,+21 describes Down syndrome; and 47,XXY describes Klinefelter syndrome.
keypoints: ⭐ Mosaic Turner patients (45,X/46,XX) often have milder stigmata and higher rates of spontaneous puberty than those with pure 45,X monosomy.
Turner syndrome is the only monosomy compatible with survival to term, likely because the fetus retains one functional X.
Cystic hygroma in utero (seen on prenatal ultrasound) reflects the same lymphatic malformation that produces the webbed neck.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman in her second pregnancy delivers a female neonate with severe generalized edema and jaundice. A CBC of the neonate shows hemolytic anemia. Subsequent workup of the mother and the newborn reveal an Rh-incompatibility. Transplacental passage of which of the following proteins is the principal cause of anasarca and jaundice in this neonate?
questions.explanation: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) is an antibody-mediated disease in which an Rh-negative mother sensitized to the D antigen by a prior Rh-positive pregnancy produces anti-D antibodies that, unlike IgM, are small enough as IgG to cross the placenta and hemolyze fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes. This fetal hemolysis and resulting anemia can precipitate high-output congestive heart failure with severe generalized edema (hydrops fetalis) along with jaundice from bilirubin release. Complement proteins C3 and C4 and interferon-alpha are not the mediators of this transplacental antibody-driven hemolysis.
keypoints: ⭐ Only IgG, not IgM, crosses the placenta, which is why the first Rh-positive pregnancy is typically unaffected (sensitization occurs at that delivery) but subsequent pregnancies are increasingly severe.
Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) given to Rh-negative mothers prevents maternal sensitization by clearing fetal Rh-positive cells before an immune response develops.
Hydrops fetalis represents the most severe form of erythroblastosis fetalis, driven by severe anemia leading to congestive heart failure.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman gives birth to a neonate with multiple congenital abnormalities. Physical findings included a flat facial profile, slanted eyes, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots, short nose, short neck, dysplastic ears, clinodactyly, a large protruding tongue, and a pronounced heart murmur. What is the most common cause of this developmental birth disease?
questions.explanation: This constellation of findings is classic for Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Nondisjunction during the first meiotic division of gametogenesis accounts for 92-95% of Down syndrome cases, with the extra chromosome 21 being of maternal origin in about 95% of these; maternal age is a major risk factor, consistent with this 42-year-old mother. Robertsonian translocation involving the long arm of chromosome 21 accounts for a smaller subset, about 5% of cases, while chromosomal deletion, trinucleotide repeat expansion, and frameshift point mutation are not mechanisms of Down syndrome.
keypoints: ⭐ Advanced maternal age dramatically increases the risk of meiotic nondisjunction and thus of trisomy 21.
Translocation Down syndrome (unlike the nondisjunction form) can be familial and carries a significant recurrence risk in future pregnancies.
Congenital heart defects (especially endocardial cushion/AV canal defects) occur in about 40-50% of Down syndrome infants.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with a history of autism and mental retardation is seen by a genetic counselor. The man has coarse facial features, an increased head circumference, and macro-orchidism. His maternal uncle is similarly affected. After further evaluation, a diagnosis of fragile X syndrome is rendered. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's genetic disease?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of mental retardation, is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in a noncoding region adjacent to the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. The expanded repeat silences FMR1 through promoter methylation and creates a cytogenetically visible "fragile site." The X-linked inheritance pattern (with a maternal uncle also affected) fits the trinucleotide repeat expansion mechanism, whereas nondisjunction, chromosome inversion, frame-shift mutation, and nonreciprocal translocation do not explain fragile X syndrome.
keypoints: ⭐ Fragile X is a trinucleotide repeat disorder, joining Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy in this mechanistic family, and can show anticipation (worsening severity/earlier onset in successive generations).
Macro-orchidism, long face, and large everted ears are classic postpubertal physical findings.
A significant proportion of boys with autism spectrum disorder carry the fragile X mutation, making it a key test to consider in male autism with intellectual disability.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents for a pregnancy test. She recalls drinking heavily during the week in which she may have conceived. What is the most likely consequence of toxic exposure to the conceptus during early (preimplantation) development?
questions.explanation: During the preimplantation stage, blastomeres are still totipotent and interchangeable, so a noxious agent that damages some cells is typically compensated for by the remaining cells, following an all-or-none principle: either the conceptus dies or development proceeds normally, without causing structural malformations. The most common consequence of toxic exposure at this very early stage is therefore death of the embryo, which often passes unnoticed or presents as delayed, heavier-than-usual menstrual bleeding; about 30% of fertilized ova are spontaneously lost this way. Neural tube defects and ventricular septal defects are errors of morphogenesis that arise from teratogen exposure at later (embryonic) stages, not the preimplantation period, and conjoined twins and placenta accreta are unrelated to this mechanism.
keypoints: ⭐ The "all-or-none" principle of preimplantation teratogenesis explains why very early pregnancy losses from toxin exposure often go unrecognized as pregnancies at all.
Roughly 30% of fertilized ova are lost spontaneously before pregnancy is clinically recognized.
In contrast, teratogen exposure during organogenesis (weeks 3-8) produces structural malformations rather than simple embryonic loss.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he falls a lot, cannot jump, and tires easily. Physical examination reveals weakness in the pelvic and shoulder girdles and enlargement of the child's calf muscles. The serum level of creatine kinase is elevated. A biopsy of calf muscle reveals marked variation in size and shape of muscle fibers. There are foci of muscle fiber necrosis, myophagocytosis, regenerating fibers, and fibrosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death expected in this patient?
questions.explanation: This is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an X-linked disorder causing relentless proximal (pelvic and shoulder girdle) muscle degeneration with calf pseudohypertrophy (fibroadipose replacement of muscle) and markedly elevated creatine kinase. Patients become wheelchair-bound by about age 10 and bedridden by age 15. Death most commonly results from respiratory insufficiency due to progressive weakness of respiratory muscles, or from cardiac arrhythmia related to associated cardiomyopathy. The other choices (aortic dissection, DIC, pulmonary embolism, rhabdomyosarcoma) are not recognized complications of DMD and are distractors unrelated to its natural history.
keypoints: ⭐ DMD is caused by frameshift/out-of-frame mutations leading to absent dystrophin, versus in-frame mutations in the milder Becker muscular dystrophy that produce a truncated but partially functional protein.
Calf 'pseudohypertrophy' reflects replacement of degenerated muscle by fat and connective tissue, not true muscle hypertrophy.
Cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia is the second major cause of death alongside respiratory failure.
⭐ Loss of ambulation typically occurs by age 10-12, with death usually in the late teens to twenties without ventilatory support.

questions.stem: Molecular diagnostic assays performed on muscle biopsy from the patient described in Question 1 would show alterations in the length of the primary transcript for which of the following muscle-associated proteins?
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from mutations (commonly large deletions or duplications) in the dystrophin gene, one of the largest genes in the human genome, located on the short arm of the X chromosome (Xp21). These mutations alter the length of the primary transcript and disrupt the reading frame, abolishing dystrophin protein expression. Dystrophin normally anchors the subsarcolemmal cytoskeleton to a transmembrane glycoprotein complex that binds laminin in the extracellular matrix; its absence increases sarcolemmal fragility, permits excess calcium influx, and causes leakage of muscle enzymes such as creatine kinase into serum. Creatine kinase, desmin, glycogen phosphorylase, and myosin genes are not altered in DMD; creatine kinase is simply a downstream serum marker of muscle damage, not the mutated gene.
keypoints: ⭐ The dystrophin gene spans about 2.4 million base pairs, making it particularly prone to deletions and duplications detectable by multiplex PCR/MLPA.
Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (including dystroglycans and sarcoglycans), which binds laminin-2 in the basal lamina.
Loss of this sarcolemma-extracellular matrix linkage increases membrane fragility and pathologic calcium entry, driving fiber necrosis.
Desmin and myosin mutations instead cause distinct myopathies (e.g., desminopathies, myosin storage myopathy), not DMD.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman complains of weakness and easy fatigability, which is most pronounced in the late afternoon. She describes difficulty reading and tiredness while watching television. She has problems chewing and swallowing and loses her voice while talking. Physical examination reveals ptosis and diplopia. Laboratory studies would most likely demonstrate serum autoantibodies directed against which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation: This presentation—fatigable weakness worsening with sustained activity or later in the day, ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria, chewing difficulty)—is classic for myasthenia gravis. It is an autoimmune disease in which circulating IgG autoantibodies bind postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction (motor endplate), reducing effective receptor number and impairing neuromuscular transmission. These antibodies can be detected serologically and localized to the motor endplate by immunohistochemistry in most patients. Phosphodiesterase, desmin, dystrophin, and troponin are not the targets in myasthenia gravis and are distractors referencing other muscle proteins/pathways.
keypoints: ⭐ Symptoms classically worsen with sustained muscle use/fatigue over the day and improve with rest, distinguishing MG from primary myopathies.
Ocular and bulbar muscles (extraocular, eyelid, pharyngeal) are affected early, producing ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia/dysarthria.
Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing and repetitive nerve stimulation showing decremental response support the diagnosis.
⭐ Anti-MuSK antibodies account for a subset of seronegative (anti-AChR-negative) myasthenia gravis cases.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with muscle weakness. He cannot open his hand for a handshake and cannot extend his arm after flexing it. On physical examination, he has marked atrophy of leg and arm muscles, ptosis, and a fixed facial expression. There is testicular atrophy. Laboratory studies demonstrate mild diabetes. A muscle biopsy reveals atrophy of type I fibers, hypertrophy of type II fibers, and numerous fibers with centrally located nuclei. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is myotonic dystrophy, the most common adult-onset muscular dystrophy, an autosomal dominant trinucleotide (CTG) repeat disorder. Its hallmark clinical feature is myotonia—delayed relaxation after muscle contraction, illustrated here by the inability to release a handshake or extend the arm promptly after flexion. Beyond skeletal muscle, it is a multisystem disease affecting the heart, smooth muscle, CNS, endocrine glands (testicular atrophy, insulin resistance/diabetes, frontal balding), and eyes (cataracts), producing the described fixed/myopathic facies and ptosis. Biopsy classically shows atrophy of type I fibers with type II fiber hypertrophy and abundant internally placed nuclei, a constant feature distinguishing it from Duchenne dystrophy, in which necrosis/regeneration predominate rather than centrally located nuclei.
keypoints: ⭐ Caused by a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, showing anticipation (worsening severity/earlier onset in successive generations).
Multisystem involvement—cardiac conduction defects, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, and insulin resistance—helps distinguish it from purely muscular dystrophies.
Centrally located (internalized) nuclei in a high proportion of fibers is a constant, near-diagnostic histologic feature.
Congenital myotonic dystrophy (from maternal transmission of a large repeat expansion) presents with severe neonatal hypotonia, distinct from the adult-onset form described here.

questions.stem: A female neonate is noted at birth to have a gross deformity of her lower back. Examination of the subcutaneous lesion reveals disorganized neural tissue with entrapment of nerve roots. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Neural tube (dysraphic) defects result from impaired closure of the dorsal vertebral column and range in severity from spina bifida occulta to meningocele, meningomyelocele, and rachischisis. Meningomyelocele exposes the spinal canal, allowing herniation of both meninges and disorganized neural tissue with entrapment of nerve roots, matching this infant's lesion. Meningocele involves only a meninges-lined fluid sac without neural tissue, spina bifida occulta is a clinically silent vertebral arch defect, and rachischisis is a more extreme defect often lacking a recognizable spinal cord. Syringomyelia is an unrelated tubular cavitation of the cord itself, not a closure defect.
keypoints: ⭐ Neural tube defect severity spectrum: spina bifida occulta (vertebral arch only, asymptomatic) < meningocele (meninges only) < meningomyelocele (meninges + entrapped neural tissue) < rachischisis (failure of neural tube closure, no distinct cord)
Meningomyelocele occurs most often in the lumbosacral region and is frequently associated with Arnold-Chiari II malformation
Syringomyelia is a distinct, non-dysraphic entity involving fluid-filled cavitation within the cord and typically presents later in life
⭐ Elevated maternal serum/amniotic alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the key prenatal screening marker for open neural tube defects

questions.stem: The parents of the neonate described in Question 1 ask about the risks for similar birth defects in their future offspring. You mention that supplementation of the maternal diet can reduce the incidence of neural tube defects. What is this important dietary supplement?
questions.explanation: Maternal folic acid deficiency is associated with an increased incidence of neural tube defects, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended in women of childbearing age and has been mandated as a fortificant in commercial flour. None of the other listed vitamin deficiencies are linked to dysraphic anomalies: niacin deficiency causes pellagra, thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke syndrome and beriberi, and vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anemia with subacute combined degeneration. Folate is essential for the one-carbon transfers needed for DNA synthesis and methylation during the critical period of neural tube closure.
keypoints: ⭐ Folic acid supplementation (400 mcg/day) started before conception reduces neural tube defect risk by up to 70%
Neural tube closure is complete by about day 28 of gestation, often before pregnancy is recognized, which is why supplementation should begin preconception
Antiepileptic drugs (valproic acid, carbamazepine) are folate antagonists and independently raise neural tube defect risk
⭐ After one affected pregnancy, recurrence risk rises substantially, prompting a higher folic acid dose (4 mg/day) in subsequent pregnancies

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man suffers massive trauma in a motorcycle accident. A CT scan shows multiple intracerebral hemorrhages. The patient expires after 6 months in a coma. At autopsy, there are cystic cavities within the frontal and temporal lobes, corresponding to the areas of prior hemorrhage. These cavities were formed in large measure due to the phagocytic activity of which of the following cell types?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic, macrophage-derived cells of the CNS and account for the clearance of necrotic tissue and hemorrhagic debris after injury, producing the fluid-filled cystic cavities characteristic of remote cerebral contusions/infarcts. Lipid-laden microglia that have ingested debris are termed gitter cells, and reactive forms with elongated nuclei are called rod cells. Astrocytes are not the primary phagocytes; instead they proliferate afterward (astrocytosis/gliosis) to wall off the cavity and form a glial scar, which is why astrocytes are a distractor here. Endothelial cells, neutrophils, and oligodendrocytes do not perform this bulk phagocytic clearance role in chronic CNS injury.
keypoints: ⭐ Microglia are of monocyte/macrophage (mesodermal) lineage, unlike astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, which are neuroectodermal in origin
Lipid-laden phagocytic microglia are called "gitter cells"; elongated reactive microglia are called "rod cells"
⭐ Sequence after CNS injury: liquefactive necrosis to microglial phagocytosis of debris to cystic cavity formation to astrocytic gliosis forming the surrounding glial scar
This liquefactive necrosis-to-cyst pattern is characteristic of CNS infarcts/contusions, contrasting with the fibrous (collagenous) scarring typical of other organs
